utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And welcome, both of you. I just want to confirm to make sure that there are no further problems with the audio and that you are receiving interpretation in a language that you understand? Okay, I see nodding. All seven parties here today have lodged appeals against the Trial Judgement rendered by Trial Chamber III on 29th of May, 2013. In accordance with the Scheduling Order of 15th December, 2016, and the order for the preparation of the appeal hearing on 1st March, 2017, the Appeals Chamber will hear the appeals this week as well as on next Monday and Tuesday. Before we begin, I will provide a very brief summary of the case before turning to the conduct of the appeal hearing. The events giving rise to the appeals in this case occurred between 1992 and 1994 in eight municipalities and five detention centre camps in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was claimed as part of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. The Trial Chamber found that Jadranko Prlic exercised duties of the president of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna as of August 1993, having earlier been appointed the president of the executive organ of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. In June 1994, he became vice-president of the government and minister of defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bruno Stojic also served in the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. He was head of the Department of Defence from July 1992 to November 1993 and subsequently headed the Department for the Production of Military Equipment until April 1995. Slobodan Praljak was the assistant minister of Defence of Croatia and later served as the deputy minister of defence of Croatia. From the 24th of July, 1993, to 9th November, 1993, he was commander of the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council, Army of BiH Croats, before returning to Croatia as advisor to the Croatian minister of defence. Milivoje Petkovic served as chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council between April 1992 and July 1993 and subsequently served as deputy commander. In April 1994, he returned to his position as chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council. Valentin Coric served in the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. He was chief of the military police administration in 1992 and most of 1993 and then became minister of the interior, a post which he held until early 1994. In February 1994, he became a member of the presidential council. Berislav Pusic occupied various posts within the military police of the Croatian Defence Council between February and July 1993, during which time he also participated in negotiations for the exchange of detainees or the bodies of the dead. By May 1993, he became a member of the exchange commission. And in July 1993, he became the head of the executive organ of the exchange commission. On the 6th of August 1993, Pusic became the head of the commission for HVO prisons and detention centres. The Trial Chamber found that by January 1993 a joint criminal enterprise had come into existence that was aimed at creating a Croatian entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina that would facilitate the reunification of the Croatian people. According to the Trial Chamber, this joint criminal enterprise had as its common criminal purpose the "domination by Croats of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna through ethnic cleansing of the Muslim population." The Trial Chamber concluded that all six Defence Appellants were participants in the joint criminal enterprise. The Trial Chamber convicted the Defence Appellants of various crimes charged by the Prosecution. These charged crimes included: 1. Grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, namely wilful killing, sexual assault, unlawful deportation, transfer and detention of civilians, inhumane treatment and extensive destruction, and appropriation of property not justified by military necessity and carried out unlawfully and wantonly; 2. Violations of the laws or customs of war, namely: Cruel treatment, unlawful labour, wanton destruction of cities, towns, or villages, destruction or wilful damage to institutions dedicated to religion or education, and plunder of public or private property; and 3. Crimes against humanity, namely: Persecutions, murder, rape, deportation, forcible transfer, imprisonment, and inhumane acts. The Trial Chamber based all of the Defence Appellants' convictions on their participation in the joint criminal enterprise and found them responsible through the basic and extended form of joint criminal enterprise liability. Coric was also found to bear superior responsibility for some crimes which occurred in 1992. Notwithstanding its findings of guilt with respect to the Defence appellants for cruel treatment and wanton destruction of cities, towns, or villages, the Trial Chamber declined to enter convictions for these crimes after considering the principles related to cumulative convictions. Praljak and Pusic were acquitted of rape as a crime against humanity and sexual assault as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions. Pusic was also acquitted of extensive appropriation of property and plunder of public or private property. All Defence Appellants were acquitted of cruel treatment as a violation of the laws or customs of war in relation to the Siege of Mostar. The Trial Chamber sentenced Prlic to 25 years of imprisonment, Stojic, Praljak, and Petkovic were each sentenced to 20 years, Coric to 16 years, and Pusic to 10 years of imprisonment. All parties have lodged appeals against the Trial Chamber for a combined total of 146 Grounds of Appeal. The Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber erred in partly acquitting the six Defence Appellants and seeks increases in their sentences. The Defence Appellants submit that they should be acquitted on all counts; and in the alternative, Appellants Stojic, Petkovic, Pusic, and Coric seek finding of reduced culpability along with a reduced sentence, while Appellant Praljak asks for a new trial. I can assure the parties that the Appeals Chamber is familiar with your written pleadings, and I would therefore ask counsel not to repeat or summarise in any extensive manner the arguments already presented in your briefs. Counsel are urged, however, to provide precise reference to material supporting their oral submissions. I should also like to remind the parties to speak slowly so as to allow the submissions to be interpreted properly. Additionally, I would like the parties to be particularly careful, and please pay attention to this, not reveal any information that could identify a protected witness or other protected information or material. The parties were invited to discuss a number of issues set out in the order of 1st March, 2017, and I would like each one of you to indicate, for the sake of clarity, which issue you will be addressing at any given time by reading out the relevant question at the start of your submission. I had hope I have made myself clear on this. It should be recalled that these appeals are not a trial de novo, and the parties must refrain from repeating their cases which were presented at trial. Article 25 of the Statute provides that the arguments on appeal should be limited to alleged errors of law that invalidate the Trial Judgement or alleged errors of fact that have occasioned a miscarriage of justice. I will now turn to today's timetable. The parties have been allotted a specific amount of time to make their submissions this week and next, set out in my order of the 1st of March, 2017. Counsel are reminded to organise their submissions in a way that adheres to this schedule. Today we will hear submissions from Mr. Prlic's counsel for a total of two hours. We will, however, have a pause of 15 minutes one hour into these submissions. After Mr. Prlic's counsel have completed their submissions, the Prosecution will have two hours to respond. As with Mr. Prlic's submissions, we will pause halfway into the Prosecution's response. This second pause will last one hour and 30 minutes. Finally after the Prosecution has responded, Mr. Prlic will have 30 minutes to reply. Lastly, I would like to note that it is customary for the Appeals Chamber to give appellants an opportunity to make a personal address to the Appeals Chamber if they so wish. And therefore, we have reserved Tuesday, 28th of March, for this purpose when each Appellant will have ten minutes to address the Tribunal. I would like now to invite counsel for Mr. Prlic to present their submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Yes, Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: I'm going to speak on my language. [Interpretation] Your Honours, after the judgement, I have read the entire transcript of the trial, compared it with the judgement, I co-operated with my Defence team in the writing of appeal documents, and only after this weekend I decided to participate in the arguments. [Interpretation] I have just completed a book as well, six volumes, 1800 pages, almost 9.000 footnotes about what was Herceg-Bosna in context. It will soon be published by the Academy for Arts and Sciences of Bosnia and Herzegovina, reviewed by three academicians. It proves completely different intentions and purposes of Herceg-Bosna, but it is a scientific study, not a story of criminal responsibility. [In English] Trial Chamber, I'm going to use just chamber. [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber concerning question 4, your question 4, failed to establish what was Herceg-Bosna. In that month of October 1993, when allegedly I became aware of the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise, the Presidency of the HZHB had a session attended by at least 22 more representatives of municipalities, more than the original 30 from the basic decision on its establishment on 18 November 1991, adopted a decision to accept the association of all Croatian communities, I quote: "Bosanska Posavina, Usora, Central Bosnia, the community of Soli and Sarajevo," 2D01262, page 16. Based on several shown documents, a map was made showing municipalities that were part of the HZHB showing that it covers most of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Please show document 1D02843 and let this document displayed throughout my presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for intervening, Mr. President, but we're already embarking on a procedure, I think, that's not certainly been approved by the Chamber or comports with the Rules and, at the very least, is going into issues that the Prosecution -- it's not clear to us the extent to which these fall within the appeal grounds and the issues that are before the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, sorry to interrupt to you, but the --

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: This is Ground 9 of our appeal, so this is absolutely clear. And I'm going just to speak about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment --

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: -- [Overlapping speakers]. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic, one moment. Mr. Stringer has raised an issue, which is not an issue at the same time, but I need to address it. Mr. Stringer, it seems that the Appellant Mr. Prlic and his counsel have agreed on the way the Defence case for purpose of this appeal is to be conducted. There is nothing in the procedure that would make it possible for me to stop Mr. Prlic from taking over and presenting the case entirely himself at the same time keeping counsel present in the courtroom in case he would like to seek advice from him. But as far as the presentation of the arguments are concerned, there is no way I can entertain your submission that this is something strange. It's something that certainly is not ruled out by our procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Prlic, you can proceed. And in addition, he is addressing some of the questions that we have put in the -- mentioned in the order of 1st of March. Yes, Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: May I proceed? Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Also, Defence Offices were formed in 46 municipalities, P00700. Instead of a couple of Tudjman quotations from 1991 taken out of context, the Trial Chamber, in formulating the alleged political purpose in paragraph 43, failed to take into account dozens, I would say hundreds, of quotations from other presidential transcripts. I don't want to enumerate them all, it would take too much time, but they are in our appeal brief, count 9. Tudjman continuously, regardless of the people he is speaking to - his internal circle, international representatives, Muslims or Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina - uses the same language supporting the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, expressing himself against any change of border, for co-operation with Muslims, against war, and he refuses annexation of Herzegovina which was offered to him by Izetbegovic. He was under pressure from the international community to change borders. The Trial Chamber also neglected all the assistance of Croatia and the HVO to the government in Sarajevo and Muslims. Why is this important?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Prlic be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber -- [In English] Yeah, yeah. I just heard. [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber failed to consider that Herceg-Bosna did not contain only the municipalities mentioned in the decision on its establishment in 1991. The so-called common criminal purpose in paragraph 43 is erroneous. That's question 4. As well as that from October Prlic and others were aware that this purpose could have been achieved only by displacement of Muslims. Herceg-Bosna in mid- January, when the common criminal plan supposedly emerged, comprised almost all the free territory of Bosnia- Herzegovina. Herceg-Bosna, without any defined borders, as well as the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, continuously, all the way up to the Federation in 1994, as its Constitution stated, contained all the majority Croat and Bosniak areas in BH, P04611, 4D01234. As Izetbegovic stressed in 1993, that part from Tuzla to Neum, you can see that on the map, contains almost 2 and a half million people under protection of partly the army, partly the HVO, P01739, page 24. The Trial Chamber failed to consider that the president of the HVO HZHB, and later the government was answerable to presidents of the municipal HVO who were members of the Presidency of the HZHB, that is to say the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, from 46 different municipalities throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and not a select club that was supposedly answerable to the alleged purposes of the JCE, 1D02816, P07410, pages 18 to 20, 1D02740. This is important for later consideration about the displacement of population and annexations of parts of territory. On behalf of all of the municipalities, the President Mate Boban, later Zubak, negotiated on all international plans on internal organisation, not division as is sometimes claimed, from the Cutileiro Plan about three constituent units, the Vance-Owen Plan concerning ten provinces, the union of three republics, up to the federation, the plan of the contact group, and the Dayton Accords. The Trial Chamber failed to establish that the mentioned Croatian communities were created as a form of organisation within the party for the purpose of defence during 1991 against the background of the breakup of Yugoslavia. If the Trial Chamber had correctly judged on the evidence, it would have concluded that the Serbian attacks on Croatia and the expansion of war throughout the Bosnia and Herzegovina have manifested the intention to create a Greater Serbia in which the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina, look at maps 3D00871, would have been a part, and that makes pointless the story about the alleged agreement in Karadjordjevo, especially since the war started after that. The Trial Chamber also neglected that the republic government did not prevent attacks on Croatia from Bosnia-Herzegovina, nor was it able to organise defence of the country, which was also admitted by Izetbegovic: "At the time when the war began, we didn't have any army at all," P00336, page 8. If the Trial Chamber had correctly judged the evidence, it would have concluded that the Croatian communities were a form of organisation within the party due to the unreadiness of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina for its own defence, ID2078. Namely, a series of meetings of the HDZ in 1991 shows sequence of preparation for defence, also seen in the regionalisation. Out of a total of 109 municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the -- it comprised 70 in eight regional communities: Travnik, Herzegovina, Sarajevo, Doboj, Zenica, Tuzla, Posavina, Bihac, Kladusa, and the area of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic, please, you need to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but the interpreter has my text. Okay, okay. Thank you. [Interpretation] In the area of all, except for Banja Luka, later armed forces were formed. [In English] Politically, character of HZHB was confirmed three days after its very establishment. Excuse me. [Interpretation] The government of Bosnia-Herzegovina concluded that it was a party organisation and activity, 2D00594. The Trial Chamber neglected, and this is very important, in establishing the alleged criminal purpose, criminal intent, and its territorial aim, that the HDZ, BH, within which communities were formed, in all its programme documents from 1990 to 1994 was always in favour for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the equality of the Croatian people within it, following the course of international negotiations, 1D02699, P0022, P0031, P08748, page 274. Also supporting this, the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with the votes of two Croatian representatives, on 20th December, 1991, addressed a demand for the international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Trial Chamber neglected that there were two conditions for the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is important for criminal intent. What was necessary, beside a referendum, was an agreement on the internal structure, organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the representatives of its constituent peoples. In this connection, the international community prepared the Cutileiro Plan accepted by all the three parties in March 1992. The declaration on principles envisaged the following: Bosnia-Herzegovina is a state made up of three constituent units based on ethnicity, taking into account in all the economic, geographic, and other criteria. The Trial Chamber neglected to consider that the Croats were tricked because they expected that with the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, voted for by the referendum, would resolve also the question of its internal organisation as promised by Izetbegovic. Izetbegovic himself admitted to tricking them. 1D02720, P00117, et cetera. The Trial Chamber neglected to consider that the HZHB was not active at all until the beginning of the war on 8 April when the military wing HVO was formed. It was the first decision after its establishment, which testifies to the purpose of the community, that is to say, defence. On the other hand, the Presidency, that is to say, Izetbegovic, mainly without the participation of Croats, formed the TO, later called the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, basically a Muslim army. With a decision on the establishment of units of Territorial Defence in May 1992, in -- 44 different units were formed, and Izetbegovic named 44 commanders; 43 Muslims and one Serb. There were no units in areas where HVO already existed on a massive scale, such as Herzegovina or Posavina. 3D00420. The Trial Chamber failed to establish reasons why the HZHB took over part of executive powers temporarily. First of all, it failed to take into account the collapse of governments in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Just three examples: The entire budget was financed from primary issue, which is economically unheard of. 1D03003. Second, unconstitutional districts were formed and they were given the entire authority. Three, the Law on Public Finance transferred to municipalities and districts the power to impose any taxes and levies and customs, 1D02047. The Trial Chamber also failed to take into account that municipalities practically became states at that time. Boban explained the reasons for taking over executive powers from September '92, I quote: "To ensure supply, trade, production, health services, the safety of citizens and their property, accommodation of refugees. Those decisions do not bring into question the sovereignty and integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina in any way. 1D2441. The president of the HVO HZHB adds: "We have to organise life on a daily basis. Our economic, financial, and any other system in Bosnia-Herzegovina has completely collapsed." The President of the BiH government agreed with that, in the same document. The Trial Chamber failed to consider that the entire development of government can be divided into three stages. In the first period, until September 1992, it was the municipalities and the HVO HZHB, municipalities and the HZHB Presidency, municipalities and HVO HZHB up to late 1993, all the way up to November 1993 when the house of representatives and the government of Herceg-Bosna became key players. And that's when the first budget was adopted for 1994. The Trial Chamber failed to take into account that the decree on rights and duties and the structure of authority of government in municipalities was taken in December 1993 and defined for the first time the rights and duties of municipalities, which at the time of Herceg-Bosna was never done, except for a perfunctory decision in June '92. In paragraph 44 the Trial Chamber concluded that in the beginning -- that in the middle of January began the so-called JCE, neglecting that on the 15th January Boban says to Izetbegovic and the co-chairman of the International Conference on ex-Yugoslavia, Berenson, Owen: "This is important: To forbid Muslims from the SDA to participate in this government. We are waiting. Spots are waiting, P1158. Muslims had rejected participation in the government and in administration. In Mostar, for instance, in a ratio of 50:50. And on the level of Herceg-Bosna, 35 per cent, to which Izetbegovic had previously agreed, 1D2546. Prlic noted in April 1993: For example, in Mostar that ratio was 5O-50, in Travnik the same. That is not the problem. The problem of mixed territories does not exist. I said before that in this area there were more Muslims living there than before the war. 1D1655, P2046. There are many decisions speaking about the participation of Muslims in government in Herceg-Bosna. I don't want to mention them all. The Trial Chamber completely neglects, and this is very important to criminal intent, that the HVO was the only multiethnic formation in that area at that time. Five months after the so-called JCE, in three brigades in the Mostar area, the number of Muslims was between 15 and 35 per cent. In the entire HVO, there were 16 per cent of Muslims. The Trial Chamber completely neglects the temporary nature of Herceg-Bosna and its activity within the -- within Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is very important for assessing CCP. HVO is a temporary body, as said in its founding document, that would exercise its powers until the moment when the regular government is established. Its temporary nature is emphasised not only in every document but also the very title of the document, that is to say, decree, not law, that would imply a statehood character. In its reporting to the Presidency of HZHB, the HVO itself calls itself a temporary organ of executive power, pending the establishment of regular government. Its temporary nature is emphasised in all public appearances. 1D02078, page 5; 1D02225, pages 2 and 3. It must be said that the judicial system of the HZHB was activated on a temporary basis and it remained within the framework of the republic legislation and structure, 1D73, 139 and 201. The Trial Chamber failed to take into account evidence indicating that Herceg-Bosna was a community of -- a collection of communities of municipalities that functioned within the legal system of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 1D02441. And this is confirmed by the president of HVO HZHB in a TV programme. I quote: "This temporary executive power was elected by presidents of the War Presidencies of the municipalities, and in that way the legitimacy is secured for that temporary executive authority. In all its documents, it notes that all of these are temporary regulations. It adopts temporary measures, respects the legislature of the republic, and in the preamble of all decisions it ties into decisions relating to the imposition of the state of war and the immediate danger of war and to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina." 1D02078, pages 4, 5. The documents that were adopted were provided to the government of the RBiH by its president. HBHZ always carried the name Bosnia and Herzegovina above its own name in all documents and decisions. The Trial Chamber also neglects my address to the Sarajevo media in March 1993. The Croatian Community is one of the foundations of the development and creation of the future Bosnia and Herzegovina and not an instrument of its destruction. Generally, the central authority in the republic does not exist. And by establishing all the instruments of authority in these areas, we have given a concrete contribution to the creation of the state of the BiH, document 1D225. Izetbegovic was aware of the character of Herceg-Bosna, which his words confirm at a press conference in Mostar on the 8th of October 1992. This is 1D02238. The Trial Chamber did not take into account that as of November 1992 by a decision of the government of the RBiH, published in the Official Gazette, the president of the HVO HZHB, that's me, the president of the government, just to be clear, represented the government of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the area of the HZHB, which meant a recognition of the temporary nature of the executive body. 1D898. There was an authorisation regarding the mentioned decision. 1D2147. I quote: "A co-ordination of all measures adopted by the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council HZHB." This is the sphere in which I acted and was recognised for. This is 1D02565. The Trial Chamber completely neglected and disregarded that Herceg-Bosna for the first time after more than 100 years established a border with the Republic of Croatia in the part of BiH where the population was practically 100 per cent Croatian. These are documents P1560, 1D2221, 1D2704, 1D -- and many others. The Trial Chamber failed to take into account evidence that the Croatian community and the Croatian republic were never states, nor did they want to be states. They did not have a defined area as can you see on the map, nor boundaries or borders. In all the founding documents, for example, the statutory decision on the executive power, it is always said "area," "podrucje," not "territory" which would imply a state character of the body. This is 1D899. Furthermore, the decree on taking over decrees with the force of law and the citizenship of BiH, the citizenship of Herceg-Bosna is not being introduced. We were all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. P7179, P7082. Herceg-Bosna never sought international recognition. To answer your question number 4 where paragraphs 283, 284 from the judgement are cited, I don't need to repeat them here, these are paragraphs relating to the drafting of the ultimatum and so on, it is important to note that the counsel, among other things -- the Chamber, among other things, failed in an adequate way to establish the responsibilities of the president of the HVO HZHB. Just like you, Mr. President, the president of the temporary organ of executive power could act only at convened meetings. P303, article 16. He had one vote in the body, the collective body of some 20 members, heads of departments and sub-departments. The president signed all decisions even though in theory he could have been against them in the same way that applies to you, Mr. President. Documents P9530, 1D2117, P303, 1D65, 1D1643. The Chamber reached erroneous decisions regarding the option of supervision of departments by the president of the HVO HZHB. It failed to consider that the departments were independent, answerable to the Presidency of HZHB, which appointed them before it appointed the president of the HVO HZHB. These are P303, Articles 2 to 22; 1D1, Articles 2 to 7; P434; 1D171; 173; 174; and 010. Had the Trial Chamber properly considered the evidence, they would have reached beyond a reasonable doubt the decision that the HVO HZHB and the government did not have military powers or the option of utilising the armed units. This is part of Ground 2 of our appeal. The Trial Chamber failed to reach the only reasonable conclusion, even though it concedes in paragraph 106 that I was not part of the chain of command but still its decision treated me as if I were. The Trial Chamber erred because it did not note that by changing the decree on armed forces in October 1992, HVO HZHB lost all its authorities regarding the armed formations, which is logical in view of the fact that Boban was no longer at the head of the HVO HZHB, Articles 30 and 34, and the armed force were financed by the municipalities. This is P289, Article 55; and P588, Article 170. HVO HZHB did not receive any security information. P128, page 19. The security service, which was formally part of the Defence Department, was financed by the municipalities. 2D931. No single document or decision provided for by Article 9 of the Decree on Armed Forces was not adopted regarding the HVO HZHB, nor was ever any plan of defence of HZHB. HVO HZHB or its president never issued a single order. Not one decision. Not one meeting was marked with any degree of confidentiality, and let me remind you all this was happening during the war. The Trial Chamber failed to take into account that I was appointed president of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina in late May 1993, four months after the alleged beginning of the JCE, with the approval of the Muslims, which is confirmed in a letter by Alija Izetbegovic on the 27th of May 1993. I quote: "We Medjugorje agreed for you to be the candidate for the first prime minister of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Document 1D1600. The Trial Chamber failed to take into account that I took measures in order to set up effective organs of authority in BiH with the intent of applying international plan of construction of a normal Bosnia-Herzegovina, attempting to include third parties in this. documents 1D from 1586 to 1602. This process included the abolishment or rather the transformation of the institutions of Herceg-Bosna into provincial or rather institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina. 3D342. In any event, I stopped being the president of the HVO HZHB and stopped coming to meetings. This is document 1609, 1608, and 1666.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Prlic. Again, my attention is being drawn to the fact that you are reading too fast for the court recorders.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We are actually not reading from the text. We are translating a Vista.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these elements are important in response to your questions 4, 5, and 10 because the Trial Chamber failed to review the alternative explanation, that the decision of the 15th of January, 1993 was adopted with the conviction that agreement was reached on a joint command following a large number of agreements which were never implemented, with the conviction of preventing conflict, and that after the demobilisation, demilitarisation would also follow as provided for under the VOPP. The Trial Chamber fails to note that the decision was reciprocal, temporary, and as it is stated in his document by the chief of the Main Staff, the commands of the armed forces of the HVO at the level of the operative zones and brigades must include officers of the ABiH proportional to the number of soldiers on the front line. This is also the implementation of the agreement on joint commands. In this document by Petkovic, there is no threatening nature as indicated in paragraph 7. The commanders of the operation zones must speak with the commands of the ABiH and find the best solutions to form joint commands. Document P1l56. There would be no logic in the HVO agreeing to the subordination of its own forces to this party it considered a threat or a hostile party. As many as 11 HVO brigades fought together with the ABiH in cantons where there was no majority Croatian population. I see 47. There was no intention to enforce this by force. P1215. It's based on practically the same elements, and it's identical to the decision issued at the same time by the defence minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina. 2D1409. The Trial Chamber neglected the fact that this decision could not have any effect on events on the ground. The only clash that occurred in that period was the one in Gornji Vakuf which began on the 11th of January. The Trial Chamber failed to conclude, and this has to do with your questions 4 and 5, and one can see this simply by looking at the documentations, that a local ultimatum was issued in Gornji Vakuf for all the trenches to be abandoned on the 17th of January, all the trenches that were facing the HVO and that were dug by the Army of the -- the ABiH, which in no way has anything to do with the decision of the HVO HDZ of the 15th of January, 1993. The command by Andric was a simple military reaction to the situation on the ground because the ABiH army placed trenches facing the HVO and blocked its movements, including its access to its own command, documents P1l85 and 1194. Document 4D348, citing Andric's command and this local one-day ultimatum, repeats points from the agreement of eight points that had to do with internal already agreed on measures, such as a cease-fire, abandoning the covering up the trenches, organisation of joint patrols, demilitarisation of the town, and so on with a deadline of implementation of 24 hours on the 17th of January, 1993. This is confirmed by documents from both side. P1163, 1174, 1182, 1206, 1220, 1226, 1236, 1D816. Andric's order explicitly stated, I quote: "apply the conditions from the cease-fire agreement of the 13th of January." This is 4D348 and 4D346. So it has nothing to do with the decision of the HVO HZHB of the 15th of January, which in all of its derivatives does not have the form of a military command, has nothing to do with the use of armed forces, and which provided for the implementation of joint commands as of the 20th of January, 1993. P1146. And a key moment, the Trial Chamber neglected that the decision of the 15th of January never went into effect, nor could it produce any kind of effect, because it was withdrawn before the deadline for its implementation. In a letter written by his own hand, Mate Boban, HZHB president, who provided the information and the order on the agreement, so that said decision of 15 January could be issued, wrote on the 20th of January, on the day it was supposed to be implemented, I quote: "I direct you in the course of the day to schedule an extraordinary meeting of the HVO HZHB and to amend item 5." HVO HZHB did exactly what Boban and Izetbegovic asked in their letter, P1267, of the 17th of January. It reached the decision to extend the deadline for its implementation until peace negotiations ended. 1D820, 1D821, 1D1655, P2046. Thus, had the Trial Chamber taken this evidence into account, it would not have, and particularly not beyond a reasonable doubt, have concluded that it constituted, I quote "agreement regarding common criminal design." This is the trial judgement paragraph 44. In the same way, had the Trial Chamber taken into account that there was no activity aimed at doing anything in order to apply the so-called ultimatum in April, the Trial Chamber would have rejected the construction arrived at on the basis of a couple of articles in the press. The Trial Chamber erred turning Boban's proposal into the firing point for a conflict to set up common commands in accordance with the VOPP, which he and Izetbegovic were given as a task by the co-presidents of the MKBJ with the implementation deadline of two weeks, which was confirmed by Owen. P2059, page 2. Other than newspaper reports from suspicious sources, as shown in ground 16.2, there is no evidence, not a single command, that anything was intended to be implemented, particularly not any kind of assault activity. The Trial Chamber failed to note that the question of the so-called ultimatum was not on agenda of any subsequent meeting of the HVO HZHB in April 1993. 2D891, 2D689. Not even in presidential transcript, including the conversations between Tudjman and Boban with Izetbegovic and international representatives. P2059, P1883. Nor was it ever mentioned in thousands of pages of the file of documents of the international conference on the former Yugoslavia nor in Owen's book nor in any report of the military section of the Croatian Defence Council. P3642, 1D2159. And all of that boiled down to conflicts in two villages in the Jablanica municipality, in which the ratio of forces was 2.500:300 in favour of the Muslim forces , as stated by ABiH Commander in Jablanica. The Trial Chamber failed to take into account that the BiH army issued orders and attacked already on the 13th of April, 1993, and then again on 14th and 15th of April at seven different locations, indicating that could have been no ultimatum issued by the HVO on the 15th April. Documents 4D1241, 83, 453, 599, 1241. The Trial Chamber did not note that on that same month, the 24th of April, Boban and Izetbegovic army commanders, together with Owen, issued a joint statement about the forming and structure of joint commands of the BiH army and the HVO and do not refer to any ultimatum whatsoever. Had the Trial Chamber correctly assessed evidence, they could not have concluded that the Croatian side unilaterally implemented the VOPP because the decision of its implementation was also adopted by the Muslim side. It was adopted at their own assembly, and already in January 1993 Izetbegovic issued the direction to the party to form provincial organs. Documents 1Dl281, 1D241, 1D31313, P946. The Trial Chamber did not review evidence that the Muslim side even -- in spite of its statement was not prepared for its implementation, going by promises that it could gain more. So instead of that, in the spring of 1993 it implemented unconstitutional districts as a typical example of its dual policy. 1D2565, 1D1972, and so on and so forth. It was impossible unilaterally to implement the Vance-Owen Plan, which was very precise and even provided for the ethnic composition of each of the provinces. Had the Trial Chamber correctly assessed the evidence, it would have established that the ABiH issued orders for attack in all municipalities, whereas there are no such orders on the HVO side. And believe me, I have gone through all the documents in existence. In both the areas with a Croatian majority, such as Prozor, Travnik, Fojnica, Vitez, Busovaca, Konjic, Jablanica, Mostar, Stolac, Bugojno, but also in Zenica, Kakanj, and Vares, and Zepca. In all of those municipalities, the HVO was the significantly weaker military force. Let's take a look at the orders existing in Prozor such as P00430, P00716, P00687; then Mostar and Stolac, P01970, 4D00035, 4D02000; and dozens of such orders to attack in all municipalities. The Chamber completely failed to consider the course of ABiH occupation and the expulsion of Croats and the HVO from the so-called provinces with a Croatian majority. It is illustrated by the chronological sequence of maps that you can have a look at in 4D00561 to -567, and then 4D0621 and -622. It is a chronological illustration of how the ABiH occupied in sequence the provinces with Croatian majority. An approximate figure of expelled Croats can be seen in 4D00567 according to the data of the office for displaced persons. When the Vance-Owen Plan was announced in mid-January and as of the -- for the date as of which the Trial Chamber found that alleged Croatian criminal plan to reduce the number of Muslims in the majority provinces came into being, the HVO controlled 88 per cent of provinces with the Croatian majority, whereas in August of 1993 when this alleged plan was implemented, the HVO was in control of less than 50 per cent. According to the statement of Kresimir Zubak, the president of the HRHB. It is 1D2340. The Trial Chamber did not consider the true capability and efforts of the HVO HZHB to combat crime and prosecute and try the perpetrators. It did not take into account that at the sessions of HVO HZHB, as the sole type of activity, there is no mention of the Banovina anywhere or any annexation of territory as well as the policy of forcible expulsion, population transfer in keeping with a particular goal, or any kind of discrimination. One does not find it in any piece of legislation as published in the Official Gazette. There is nothing to contravene the Geneva Conventions. There is nothing discriminatory against anyone. Such regulation can be found in P00947 and P05166. Also, all public addresses, all discussions, all internal meetings were dedicated to fully respecting international humanitarian right in an attempt to influence all those responsible to abide by the principles. All statements that were made were against transferring people and in order to secure their rescue in order to enable free movement of humanitarian convoys. In any case, there's no evidence that I could have approved a single one or deny a single one. It also includes closing down the detention centres, which actually took place owing to the decisions of the competent bodies. We can see that in P03560, P03673, and dozens of other documents. Combatting crime is something else that the Trial Chamber failed to consider, and it can be seen on the agenda of all the meetings of the HVO HZHB. For example: "In the area of the judiciary, we need to design such criminal prosecution policy that would be aimed at strictly sanctioning the perpetrators of particularly grave crimes such as murder, theft, and robbery." It is P04276. Due to continuing efforts, after lengthy preparations, as part of the Spider Operation, dozens of arrests were carried out. The principal responsibility lay with the independent judicial institutions of the HRHB soon to be integrated in the federation in order to prosecute the most serious types of crimes, including war crimes. It is 1D01249, 1D01256, 1D01251, and so on and so forth. The Trial Chamber neglected to consider the efforts of the government in order to establish an independent judiciary based on the principle of the three branches of government. The judicial branch was supposed to be particularly independent of the legislator by the legislation having no say in the appointment of prosecutors and judges in the HRHB. There was an independent judicial council in place to do that. P4611, 1D976, P7165. The copies of criminal cases registers indicate that the courts properly addressed this topic. P document P100 and document 101. The Trial Chamber failed to consider that the federation took over all cases, documents, and archives from the judiciary of the HB in order to ensure the continuity of the judicial proceedings. One needs to add that the judiciary was the first one to be constructed when the federation was created owing first and foremost to the personnel from the government of HRHB for assumed functions in the federation government. This is 5D05024, 5D05027, and so on and so forth. As you all know -- I was there -- under the Rome Rules of the Road from February 1996, the Prosecutor's Office here took over the responsibility of evaluating the justification of all indictments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic, you have seven minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: Seven?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Seven minutes. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: Have you excluded questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Seven minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber failed to consider the difference between prisons and detention centres over which the HVO HZHB had no authority. The military and civilian prisoners were there to accommodate persons who were currently on trial or who received their final judgements. Detention centres, on the other hand, were aimed at accommodating war prisoners, and this difference was pointed out at the meeting of the HRHB government of the 6th of September 1993. The conclusion was that it was assessed that the responsibility for the current situation does not lie with the HVO HZHB. It is P04841. I will skip the part now that I intended to read out concerning detention centres. The Trial Chamber also failed to consider that the Croats accepted all peace plans, as the only party to do so with the sole wish of creating a sustainable Bosnia-Herzegovina. Each one of those plans was based on the same principles; that is, to preserve Bosnia-Herzegovina and not to acknowledge any kind of population movement. All of them were based on the 1991 census. What was the sense to go against that if you look at the map from the beginning of the presentation as promoted by the Croatian community and the Croatian republic? Because that map was used to create the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It makes no sense to conclude otherwise. All those who left their homes, which is again something that the Chamber failed to consider, were allowed to go back to their home during my work in the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were allowed to return, and take back their apartments in majority Muslim areas, where permanent decisions were made to that effect, as opposed to the decree of Herceg-Bosna which did not allow for such possibility. The Chamber failed to reach the only reasonable conclusion. There was a decree in place which attempted to co-ordinate the differing municipal practices and tried to rectify the discriminatory nature of the republican law. As such, it had nothing to do with the illegal evictions as a criminal activity, because in Article 3 is regulated that an apartment cannot be assigned on a temporary basis if its former tenant was the victim of ethnic cleansing. There are five volumes of lists of tenants by the public housing enterprises in Mostar indicating that most of such abandoned properties in Mostar were assigned to Muslims. It is 3D01027. The Chamber also erred in concluding that there was a reverse ethnic cleansing. If you look at the map, it makes no sense. The official policy was for everyone to remain in their homes. P01015, 1D01824, P08155. Evacuations were carried out for -- because of danger and to avoid humanitarian disasters when there were attacks by ABiH assisted by Mujahedin forces. An example of that is the letter of Bishop Komarica requesting urgent -- that Croats from Vares be urgently rescued. If anyone wanted people to remain in their homes, it was the wish of the Catholic church. The Chamber failed to consider that Herceg-Bosna guaranteed the return of property to its rightful owners. We prevented any changes of demographic structure during the war by adopting measures to the effect that everyone should return to their places of domicile as of 1st of April, 1992. On top that, my government decided that there should be a ban on the trade of immovable property during the war, and this is 1D01892, P01580, and P01652. The Chamber failed to take note that the formation of the Croatian republic was simply an adjustment to -- of the international plan on the union of the three republics and not to implement the alleged JCE. It also failed to take notice that the Muslims established their own Muslim republic of Bosnia in keeping with the same plan, signing an agreement with the Serbian side on the factual dissolution of Bosnia-Herzegovina in September 1993. It is 1D01436, 1D01778, and 4D01040. We can also look at the numerous documents about the decision on joint command. As of the very moment of its existence, the HVO was a legal component of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Izetbegovic himself commanded the HVO in trying to lift the siege off Sarajevo. These were two components of the same armed forces enjoying the same rights under the law when it comes, for example, to pensions, benefits, or commendations. In 2D1183, the law of the Federation, we can read that the overall war, and I quote, "was a defensive war of liberation/homeland war lasting from 18th of September, 1991, until the 23rd of December 1995." Only one quarter of the overall period was the period when there was any conflict between the HVO and the ABiH. Ultimately, the Trial Chamber failed to take note of something you noticed, Mr. President, that I became the minister of defence of the ABiH as well, in the first half of '94, following which the two components carried out decisive liberation operations that brought about peace. Unfortunately, my soldiers too died before that in Srebrenica. [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prlic. We will have a break of 15 minutes now, and then I'll give you the floor Mr. Karnavas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you have one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. And again, good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Given that Dr. Prlic went into the weeds, I'm going to do a tour d'horizon demonstrating the gross errors that were committed by the Trial Chamber. That a Trial Chamber would examine all relevant evidence objectively in rendering a judgement is an article of faith that we all accept. But in this instances, in this particular case, it is manifestly false. Beneath the surface of the six volumes that the Trial Chamber produced, you have a pattern of calculated neglect of evidence, abject disregard of context, and with all due respect, a reckless abandonment of fairness. The Trial Chamber committed a number of significant and systematic errors throughout the trial and in rendering the trial judgement: It miss applied the applicable law; it selectively relied the evidence; it misinterpreted some of the evidence it selected to rely on; and more chillingly, it ignored relevant evidence which, when considered, invalidates the Trial Chamber's findings of facts and conclusions of law. And that is the crux of our appeal. Effectively, we put on a case, three Judges sat there -- four, actually, they had 26 months to write a judgement, and they ignored the entire Prlic Defence, and this is demonstrated in their judgement. By blatantly and wantonly failing to consider the evidence, the Trial Chamber failed to appreciate that while some evidence may look good, is alluring on the surface, if you scratch beneath it, if you look beneath it, it is far from reliable; while other evidence that may seem unreliable at first glance, when considered in conjunction with other evidence tends to be reliable. And what do I mean by that? Because we're going to get to some examples. When a Croat comes and testifies for the Defence, if he says: "I'm acquainted with the accused," that is taken as he is biased, he is untrustworthy, there is no need to consider the evidence from that particular witness, and we see that in the judgement with absolutely no assessment, none whatsoever, of the testimony that they gave to see whether it stands up to scrutiny. It's just: Well, he was acquainted with the accused and therefore, if we want to translate it, Croat equals liar if testifying on behalf of the Defence. That's the crux of our appeal, Your Honours. And I -- with all due respect, I understand we are at an international criminal tribunal, and as President Meron has indicated -- or Judge Meron has indicated when he was president, that we are to uphold the highest of international standards before this Tribunal, and this Trial Chamber failed, and failed miserably, and failed repeatedly in this particular trial and in the judgement which it took 26 months to create. By misapplying the proper legal standards and proper methodology in assessing the evidence, the Trial Chamber reached erroneous findings of facts and conclusions of law. They indiscriminantly ignored virtually the entire Prlic Defence, compartmentalising the evidence, assessing it out of context, devoid of other relevant evidence, making uncorroborated pronouncements. In -- the Trial Chamber repeatedly failed to provide -- the Trial Chamber repeatedly failed to provide reasoned opinions, and that's what a judgement is all about. It's about reasoned opinions. Why? Why is that essential? For two reasons. One, we have a second instance. If I don't have a reasoned opinion, how can I possibly point to the Appeals Chamber where the errors are? And two, how can you, Your Honours, do your job if there are no reasoned opinions as to how a Trial Chamber reached a particular conclusion after supposedly assessing the evidence? What is the purpose - what is the purpose - of the United Nations providing funds for Defence counsel to represent the accused, because they have a right to be represented when they cannot afford their own Defence, provide these facilities, allow us to make a record, a record, and then disregard the record, take it out of context, cherry pick what you may in order to fit desired narrative. That is the crux of our appeal. And by the way, Your Honours, while I'm at it, if you look at our appeal, because we had some -- we had some difficulties in finding -- in the word space. We were counting words in this particular process. So you will note that for every assertions that we make, every single assertion, there is a footnote. And if you look at the footnote, there are citations, page number and lines, and there is no space in between. And the reason for that was because if you have a space if counts as a word. So we could have 10, 20, 30, citations to the record and only count as one word by not having a space. Now, why was that necessary? Because we wanted to give you not the haystack but the needles in the haystack in order for you to actually go and see. Because we submit, Your Honours, that when you look at our appeal brief and when you look at documents that are cited, for every single assertion will you see a footnote, and at -- relevant lines that you need to focus on that establishes the validity of the assertion. Something that we would have expected the Trial Chamber to do when it was supposed to be doing its own job. And now you are faced with a conundrum. And what is that? By not having a reasoned opinion, not having reasoned decisions throughout, just pronouncements, now effectively, what we are asking you to do, regrettably, is to do a review de novo of 52.967 pages of a trial transcript, 818 written decisions, 5.926 exhibits. These were admitted during the course of the trial. This is effectively what you have to do, or at least look at what we cited and the other parties cited in order to determine whether Trial Chamber properly assessed the evidence. Yes, there is -- as I said, there is a rebuttable presumption that the Trial Chamber evaluated all of the evidence. That goes without saying. Now, how was it done in this particular case? Well, if we mention a name, Prlic Defence calls one witness, we'll find a way to put him in some place, maybe on some inconsequential validation of a date that is unrelated to the actual substance of the Trial Chamber; therefore, if we do a word check, we can see, oh, this person was mentioned, ergo, they considered. They considered the testimony of -- of the witness. When, in fact, I dare say, Your Honour, with all due respect, that's a subterfuge. You sprinkle the names, you sprinkle the documents, you don't do a proper assessment but then you can say, well, we did our job. We assessed the evidence. And I will show some concrete examples. It is shocking, it is scandalous. The Trial Chamber erroneously found the existence of a JCE. The purpose of establishing the HZHB and the HRHB, that's the Croatian community and the Croatian republic -- in fact, when you look at the judgement, they conflate the two. They don't even know -- at times they get confused themselves. They don't know what is one and what is the other. They failed to consider, for instance, that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established as result of the negotiations that were ongoing. By not looking at the evidence, by not assessing the evidence properly, by not considering what the witnesses were saying, by not looking at the documents. They say, oh, this is a continuation of this joint criminal enterprise that started supposedly back in 1991, December 27. They look at a presidential transcript, they focus on one or two passages out of a 125-page document -- this is before BiH, by the way, is declared independent. They have a couple of witnesses, one is the so-called expert witness, which I will get to, Ribicic from Slovenia. And they exclude everything else. They don't look at the transcripts. They don't look at the other presidential transcripts. They don't look at the other events that follow. They say, hah, on this date, the Croats are talking about BiH and what may happen. And if you look at the transcript, there are all sorts of ideas that are being bounced around. Why? Why? The context that we brought in, Your Honours, which the Trial Chamber failed to consider, was at that point in time in history it was unclear whether BiH would survive as a state. And the issue was if BiH fails, should Croatia take care of its people and its borders. And that was the discussion. But once BiH declared independence, the first country to recognise BiH was Croatia. Croatia was pumping in the arms. In fact, the Mujahedin came through Croatia. Arms, humanitarian, the refugees that were bringing in, all of this was coming from Croatia. Why would you arm the ABiH when arms go all over the place if, at the same time, the objective is to exterminate the Muslims or ethnically cleanse them from a particular area? It doesn't make sense. Yet, the Trial Chamber never bothered to take that into consideration. They disregarded the evidence on all of that. They failed to look at the critical documents on how the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna was established. They failed to take into context what was happening in situ at the time. Central bank isn't functioning. We brought in a witness. Was that considered? No. The electoral grid wasn't working? Why is that important? Well, without a payment bureau system, the money cannot go around. The municipalities are trapped on their own, and now they have to fend for themselves. And what do the Croats do that is so evil, so malevolent, so criminal? They do the same thing that the Muslims do in the Muslim-dominated municipalities, because everyone had to fend for themselves. In fact, every municipality set up its own Territorial Defence based on the All People's Defence, and they were supposed to take care of themselves. Who was going to pay the salaries? Who was going to keep schools open? Who is going to pick up the garbage? Who is going to pay pensions? Who was going to take care of anyone? The Prosecution's theory was, well, they're Croatising everything. And while the Trial Chamber didn't go that far, they certainly disregarded all of this relevant evidence that we brought in contextually. We brought in an expert, Cvikl, in order to show, at least to educate, to educate the members of the Trial Chamber what the system was and how it evolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, sorry to interrupt you. But, Registrar, could you please make sure that they stop this drilling because it's annoying me and it is disturbing everyone here. I'm sure it is disturbing everyone. All right? Until we are sitting, they have to hold it, okay? Thank you. Yes, my apologies to you Mr. Karnavas. You may proceed, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No problem. I hadn't even noticed it, to be honest. But now that you point it out, I'm aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why you haven't become a Judge as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't think I have the judicial temperament, Your Honour, with all due respect. I'd love to be one but I'm not qualified from that perspective. What we're seeing, Your Honours, is that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have reached the conclusions that they reached because they ignored virtually the entire Defence case. And it was necessary to look at how the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna was set up to start with, what was happening, and why was it set up. But by ignoring the evidence, the Trial Chamber manufactured a false narrative, and a false narrative is that Dr. Prlic was at the political apex with boundless authority over political, social, humanitarian, and military matters in the areas that were designated as a Croatian community and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. And that -- in that position, he made a substantial contribution to the joint criminal enterprise which, according to the Trial Chamber, began back in, the genesis of it, the germination of it, was in 27 December, 1991. Failing to take into account everything else that goes on including, for instance, the Friendship and Co-Operation Agreement between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tudjman and Izetbegovic. As soon as BiH is declared independent, the two leaders meet, they enter into this agreement. And if you look at the purpose of it was to find a way to organise the internal affairs, the internal administrative affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, why was this critical? And this is something that was lost on the Trial Chamber. They don't recognise it, at least not when it comes to the Croats. You have three constituent nations or peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was always recognised. That was always recognised before the war and during the war. But there's one catch for the Croats: They're in the minority, and they're always going to be in the minority. They're 17.2 or .3 per cent at the time. So how do you organise the internal affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina so you don't have the one person, one vote? Because if the Muslims, now called Bosniaks, are in the majority, they control everything. They control the president, they control the Assembly. They can have -- fill in all the administrative positions. But by recognising the -- that you have three constituent nations, not minorities but nations, they have to share in the administration of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now we saw something just last week, for instance, two weeks ago, when Izetbegovic, the son of Alija, who inherited the father's throne of the party, he goes to the International Court of Justice just down the street and he files a request for the reconsideration of a decision that was made by the International Court of Justice. Now, the problem is -- and he appoints someone as if that person is the agent of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We have an international who joins him -- or two internationals, one of them is it Shepard, David Sheppard [phoen] who is an American former ambassador, who ought to know better because he represented himself as being the deputy agent and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stick to this case, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm making a point, Your Honour. The point is that the Trial Chamber disregarded, disregarded the evidence that the Croats wanted to make sure that their rights were protected. And you have the Cutileiro Plan, you have the Vance-Owen Plan, you have the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, and so on, and all were basically of the same milieu. The Trial Chamber never considered that the Croats never presented a single plan or single map where they were arguing or claiming that this area or territory belonged to them. The maps and the plans came from the internationals. They didn't come from the Croats. And that was the whole point of the January 15 decision, which I'm going to get to in a second. Why is that important? And it's important for your question 4 but also in general with respect to the JCE. The Vance-Owen Peace Plan kicks in sort of towards the end of 1992. In January, beginning of January, I believe it's the 2nd, and then again on the 10th, there are Plenary Sessions in Geneva, where the plan already is out, and it talks about you're going to have seven to ten provinces, and depending on who is in the majority in those provinces they will be allocated. So I believe it was 3, 8, and 10 were going to be allocated, for administrative purposes, to the Croats. In other words, they would have ability to administer those provinces. It did not call for ethnic cleansing. None of the international plans, starting from Cutileiro, ever called for carving up or ethnic cleansing or movement of populations. Be that as it may, that's around the 2nd to the 10th the plan is being discussed. Meanwhile, for whatever reason, around the 2nd or 3rd in the area of Gornji Vakuf there is a scrimmage. There's some fighting going on. And it's localised. It's over the flag, over new years, whatever the case may be. Some drinking. But by the 11th, by the 11th of January, these two parts of the forces of -- of BiH, because at this point, remember, you have the Friendship and Co-operation Agreement which says that the ABiH, the Army of BiH, and the HVO are integral parts of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And so now in this localised area, you have two components of those two forces who are going at each other on the 11th, and it looks like it's going to escalate. And there's a need to find a solution. So after on January 15 or 14 when they were in Geneva, Izetbegovic travels to Zagreb and there's a meeting with Tudjman, Izetbegovic, and there's Susak there, Praljak I believe was also there, and there there's an agreement that is reached. And it's the Zagreb Agreement. And based on the Zagreb Agreement, the HVO will subordinate itself in the Muslim-dominated areas and vice versa, the BiH will subordinate itself, you know, to the HVO in the Croat-dominated areas. That's the agreement. Praljak gets this and travels from Zagreb to Mostar, and I believe most of Your Honours have been there, have travelled there at one point or another. When General Praljak leaves, the agreement is what it is. Now, whether Izetbegovic changed his mind later on, who knows. But when General Praljak arrives in Mostar, he provides -- he shows them the agreement. And based on that you could say, effectively, Boban is ordering, as he did later on on the 20th, for an extraordinary session so that this agreement could be implemented. Why? Why? Because there was fighting going on and it was getting out of control in Gornji Vakuf. That is the critical aspect. That is why the January 15, 1993, Zagreb Agreement, and then which led into the decision, and then the following orders. If you look at the orders, Your Honour, you don't see anything that followed the decision. You don't see anything about -- that would lead you to believe that this was an ultimatum. This was all made up. This is a nice phrase, "it's the ultimatum." Ultimatum on what? Because by the 20th, Boban issues another order: Withdraw that. But how do you make the linkage? Because remember in the judgement the Trial Chamber says you have the -- you have the JCE starting as of 27 -- or the common plan that we're going to reconstitute the borders of Banovina 1939 either so that Croatia takes this part or it becomes sort of a mini state, a state within a state. This starts in December 27, 1991. How do you connect, how do you link that with the decision of 15 January 1993? There's no linkage. That decision is based on the Zagreb Agreement, which is based on the fighting that's going on in situ. Where is -- I mean, what part of that did the Trial Chamber not get? Because we presented copious evidence as to what was happening, why it was happening. In fact, we brought in a witness, Batinic. And what did they say about him? Let me get to him right away since I'm talking about him, because this is kind of fascinating. This tells you a little bit about what we had to face in this particular trial. With Batinic, who was in Gornji Vakuf at the time when this fighting was happening, and he comes and he testifies. He was here four days. The Trial Chamber claim that it would explain that he did not -- I mean, here it is. They observed that: "Although his testimony appeared to lack credibility on certain points..." On certain points. Which points? We never know. "... particularly concerning the role of the HVO..." Okay. "... in the criminal events alleged to have an occurred in 1993." Well, which part? Where? Where was the assessment? Where was he found not credible? Give us an example of what he said or one document he was shown or something that you could say he is not credible because it's either his own imagination and there's no independent indicia of reliability, or there's all this other evidence that shows that what he say is not credible. Nothing, zero. That's the extent of the evaluation of the analysis of this particular witness who was in situ talking about Gornji Vakuf in relation to the 15 January, 1993 decision, which feeds in right into your question 4 in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Chapter and verse, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Chapter and verse. This is in volume 2, paragraph 308. That is where this comes from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is in Ground 2. I invite your close scrutiny and attention, your close scrutiny and attention to that particular Ground because we point out, since I'm at it I might as well go for it, we point out all of the missed opportunities that the Trial Chamber had in trying to connect our evidence to the alleged crimes in the indictment. Because, for instance, with Perkovic, and this is far -- and this is from far too many paragraphs, but I've listed on him, and it's in Ground 2, there are 17 different areas which he spoke of that are completely ignored. Tomic has 22. Now we get to Buntic, who was invited by the Trial Chamber to stay extra, this was a man that was dying of cancer and passed away, regrettably, shortly thereafter. Yet he came here with the expectation that he would testify four days like everybody else and I believe he testified nine days. Now, let's just see what they do with him. And this is in volume 1, para 511, footnote 1246. The Trial Chamber claimed that, "it would explain that it did not find Zoran Buntic's testimony concerning the structure of HZ HB very credible." That was it. "It would explain." Well, I looked, I looked, and I looked in the six volumes. And not only is his testimony primarily ignored completely, but they never make an assessment or they never explain anywhere why they didn't find his testimony credible. What parts of it they didn't find credible. Based on what evidence they didn't find it credible? I'll give you one more example because if we were to go through the Trial Chamber, I would need about a week to go through that to show you all the missed opportunities and errors that they created. The other one is Zelenika, another critical witness for us. He came and testified. I believe he was here four days. "Broadly speaking, the Chamber disregarded the testimony of witnesses whose credibility seemed doubtful throughout the session." This is a general statement now, "broadly speaking." Now, what does that mean? How can you take make an assessment, Your Honour, on whether somebody's testimony was actually considered when you have such a lame, with all due respect, pronouncement that, broadly speaking, they disregarded those whose credibility seemed doubtful. Based on what? For example, now, now we are going to get the example regarding Mirko Zelenika, in relation to whom the Chamber found that only some documents tendered through him in the hearing and subsequently admitted carried probative value. That's in volume 1, paragraph 286. So that is the extent of the evaluation. Now, he testified. Can I just say that some of the documents were not -- did not have the probative value that they would have liked. Which documents are they? Pertaining to what issues? And what on God's earth does a document have to do with his testimony? Because he came and he testified about events, what he saw, what he perceived, what he did. What about his testimony? Why was his testimony not evaluated or assessed? And which documents did they assess where they found to have carried little probative value? This is not, Your Honours, I dare say, a transparent way of evaluating and assessing the evidence. And we point out in the Ground 2 that they did this systematically with 18 of our witnesses, and we have chapter and verse, page and line. You have it all. That's why I don't want to spend what little time I have - and you have been generous - but I don't want to spend my time saying how many errors were made because there's so many of them. But let's go to the OTP witnesses because we just heard that with Batinic at least, they didn't want to consider him because he was too close to the accused. Now we get to Tomljanovich, the Prosecution's own expert analyst, call him what you will. Tomljanovich testified for several days. It was more than a week. Now, it's interesting that Tomljanovich works for the OTP, works for them for several years, I believe since 1999. I could be wrong on the date, but he worked for them for many years, and he helped prepare -- he helped question witnesses. He helped prepare the drafting of the indictment, and then after drafting the indictment, guess what? He writes his expert report. Now, tell me that's not confirmation bias. Would he dare write something other than to support the indictment that he first helped write and also to assist his paymaster, the OTP. This is their analyst. He testified. I cross-examined him. And it was a delight. And I invite you -- you know, I invite your close scrutiny and attention to that part of the transcript, because by the end of his testimony, he lacks credibility completely. He demonstrates a profound ignorance of that which he claimed to have in order to write about the creation and the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And what do we see? Do we see in the judgement anything about, well, they considered the fact that he was an OTP but nonetheless they found him credible because of X, Y, Z? No. Not a mention. Zero. Not only that. What's curious about this, this OTP employee, they don't mention, not one iota, his testimony. Not one iota. But his entire report comes in. They reference his report. Where is the analysis? Where is -- where is the assessment that based on the testimony, based on his close association -- I point to that because you see a double standard. One standard for Defence witnesses; if they're closely associated with the accused, they must lack credibility. But someone who is an employee of the Prosecution, they don't factor that into the analysis and we submit that that is utterly unfair. Ribicic was another example. He came in as an expert witness. He had testified in Kordic. In Kordic he had prepared a report. He had prepared a report which was later on turned into a book, and the thesis was that the Croatian Community, then Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, were a mini-state, and so on and so forth. Part of his -- part of his analysis or, I would say, the primary factor of his -- the tipping point was, reading the presidential transcript of 19 -- of 27 December 1991, he says this. His evidence, it's there for everyone to see. Now, at that point when he wrote that report for Kordic, that was the only transcript -- there may have one or two other transcripts available. Later on, a lot of the presidential transcripts, Tudjman's recordings, became available - became available - meaning that by the time he comes to testify in this particular case, they're available to the public. The Prosecution has them. Do you think that the Prosecutor might ask him, Hey, by the way, don't you think you ought to review these other transcripts to see whether you would change your mind? No. Not one bit. Is that factored into the Trial Chamber's analysis of Ribicic? No. But they accept his report from Kordic. We submit that that is improper, that is not the sort of -- an analysis and scrutiny that one would use in going through the evidence presented to them in order to find a proper decision. Your Honour, Mr. President, how much time do I have left? Sorry to trouble you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Half an hour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have 14 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I tried. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Wonderful. Wonderful. Thank you very much. I thought so -- my watch was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, no, 24 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Good. Your Honour, context is important, and the Trial Chamber erred massively and repeatedly and they erred unjustifiably. Now, why was context important? Because when you take something out of context, when you don't look at the historical, the political, the social context in which events are taking place, you cannot reach the proper conclusion. You cannot just assess the evidence in a vacuum. These cases are not your typical cases of street crime back home. There was a lot of things at play.
