And so when you're going to say that by organising yourself, a peoples -- constituent peoples organising themselves in areas where they are living when the state doesn't have a functioning banking system, doesn't have a functioning electrical system, nothing is being paid, they don't have a defence to speak of, parts of the country are cut off, and to say that that somehow has some nefarious purposes behind it without looking at the entire context, you're missing the point. And that's what happened here. They compartmentalise the evidence. Now, I don't know whether it was done intentional, whether they were unable to do it. Maybe they just didn't want to do it. But the bottom line is they had 26 months to get it right. They had 26 months. And we did the same thing, by the way, that we did with the Appeals Chamber, lest there be any mistakes. We like to give the needles, not the haystack. In fact, in my closing argument, my client was furious with me because I didn't do a fire and brimstone-type of closing argument, nothing to move the Chamber to tears, or what have you. Instead what I did was I went to the particular issues and I pointed out to the Trial Chamber where -- which documents they needed to look at in order to reach the right conclusion. After that, Dr. Prlic, in the end, you saw -- you heard what he said earlier. In his allocution, he said, Just look at everything. Look at the evidence. Assess it properly. It was not done in this particular case, Your Honour. You cannot say with any degree of credibility that this was a reasoned opinion. And I indicated why we need reasoned opinions. You're not expected to do a de novo review, nor did I say are you -- can you do it in a sense because then you would substituting your evaluation of the evidence. That's not what an Appeals Chamber is for. You can look at the evidence that was missed and say, Yeah, well, someone can come with another alternative explanation, and that's what we did. We pointed out to the evidence in -- that was considered, that was in the record, and said based on this, if you look at all of this evidence, no trier of fact could come to this conclusion. And, by the way, the alternative plausible explanations, alternative plausible conclusions that you can reach which show that Dr. Prlic was not a member of a JCE, there was no JCE, and certainly when it comes to the January 15th decision, that decision had nothing to do with what was happening in Gornji Vakuf or what happened on or about the 18th or 19th of January, 1993. And to suggest that somehow - somehow - Praljak travels from Zagreb, he comes to Mostar with this decision, with this agreement, and now the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, these folks that were sitting there that have no power over the military, they can't order anybody, okay, they seized the moment. They sized the moment by, Let's implement the joint criminal enterprise. That's what the Trial Chamber is suggesting with its decision of January 15, 1993. It is ridiculous. It is utterly ridiculous. No trier of fact can come to that conclusion if you go beyond the surface and actually look at the evidence, look at it carefully, and not do what the Prosecution has suggested which is, well, just toss out all of Prlic's claims because, you know, the Trial Chamber has already established that. Yes, we know the Trial Chamber established it. But how? How was it established? I want to talk a little bit about the Mladic diaries because it's another vignette, I would say. Mladic is at large. He's hiding all over the place, but they finally manage to get control over his diaries. And this is after the conclusion of the trial, or most of the evidence, so the Prosecution moves to re-open the evidence in order to bring portions of the Mladic diary. All right. We fought it. But we said, Okay, if you allow that in, those sections to come in, we want as well, keeping in mind that they have the burden of proof. We've demonstrated, Your Honours, and I think the record is rather clear - you make up your minds - whether we were diligent or not diligent, and I dare say we were diligent. We were excessively diligent. We pointed out the sections of the Mladic diaries that we wanted in. Judge Antonetti, for all his faults - and he had many of them during the trial; I'm not going to sugar-coat it - in that instance he went through every portion of the diary that we wanted and he assessed it, and he said yes. I think we got almost 90 per cent of what we asked. He said, There's a reason why I would allow this to come in. It's reasonable. It's appropriate. It rebuts what the Prosecution says. We should at least consider it. The other two, the other two said no. Okay. Now, what's wrong with the Mladic's diaries? Aside from giving -- letting the Prosecutor use it and not letting the Defence, aside from that there's one passage in the Mladic diary. Now, remember, Mladic is out there. He's writing things and nobody can seriously know whether he is being truthful, even in his diary because -- and the diary is hearsay. He is not here. It's an out-of-court statement offered for the truth, where supposedly General Praljak says, We're going for Banovina 39, or just Banovina. Of course that affects us because we're part of this joint criminal enterprise. General Praljak wants to testify. He says, Look, I'm available. I want to testify. I want to give evidence on this issue, what happened. He was there. He was present. He spoke. He had testified already. What did the majority say? This is a shocker now. I'm glad you're sitting. Because they say: The lawyers can address it in their final brief or in their closing argument. The lawyers can address what General Praljak has to say in their closing argument or their final brief. One of the Judges authored the book "Human Rights in Criminal Procedure." That same author was a Professor of Law and Procedure in the University of Zurich. That same author was President of the European Commission of Human Rights. Now, anyone who takes a basic course - a basic course - in trial advocacy knows that what comes out of the mouth of a lawyer, like me, for instance, right now, is not evidence. I wish it were but it's not evidence. So when a lawyer is asked to testify on behalf of the client, when the client is saying, Hey, I've got rights, I want to give evidence. And my client -- my client's fate hangs in the balance and they say, Well, have the lawyer give evidence. That is so scandalous it's beyond the pale. So when you look at this, this is a good example of how can you possibly say, Oh, and by the way, this whole bit about what Praljak said and the Banovina and all of that, that comes in -- that's in the judgement. We see it in the judgement. So not only are we deprived of our right to confront a witness, a major violation of Dr. Prlic's human rights; but at the same time they use this out-of-court, unsubstantiated hearsay piece of evidence in support of their theory, the Prosecution's theory, of this joint criminal enterprise, and that somehow 1991 -- I believe this even happened in 1992, that they are all connected, that we can connect the dots. And this is a representation of Dr. Prlic having a lot power, being close to the government, and furthering this plan, which ultimately becomes the criminal plan, starting with January 15, 1993. This is not assessment of evidence, Your Honours. This is not a fair trial. These are errors - these are errors - that one would not expect of a Trial Chamber in an international criminal tribunal. This trial was five years in the making. Now, of course, you could say, Well, all right, if we throw joint criminal enterprise out the door, what are we left with? Maybe we can do an assessment and to revise and to look into other modes of liability. It's been -- you know, that topic has come up in the past. Well, I dare say, as I did earlier, that's not really much of an option. And you've already discussed this. I know Judge Meron has commented on it in the Gotovina decision; Judge Robinson has also commented on it. And also a new trial would not help either. Having a new trial, when you had five years of a trial already, the accused have already been in -- the appellants, my client, has already been in ten years or more. The next trial is going to take another five years. The Dutch government won't allow anybody to be provisionally released while they're in the Netherlands, if you're from the ICTY, because that was the -- that's the agreement. It would be cruel and unusual punishment, actually, to go through a new trial, and frankly I don't know if I have the stamina to go through another trial. So I don't think that alternative modes of liability is a solution or a new trial. The only solution that you have is to reverse, because the errors are systematic and they're massive. Now, I have a little bit of time left so I want to talk just very briefly about the Siljeg -- this is part of 4(c)(i), I believe, the Siljeg reports. These came in through bar table. The Prosecutor questioned Siljeg prior to the trial, pre-trial. He was available. They never called him as a witness. They never called him as a witness. The Trial Chamber never reached out to call him as a witness, to see whether he could explain, Why would you send these reports to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. What is the connection? Are you subordinated to them? There is not one shred of evidence that shows, nothing that shows, that he had a responsibility to report to them or they had any authority over him. More importantly, there's no evidence, Your Honours. There's no evidence that those reports ever made it to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. You have to remember the conditions at the time, and you don't have any discussions of those reports during the meetings of the government. So I dare say trying to connect the Siljeg to Dr. Prlic or the HVO HZHB, there's no linkage. The Prosecution has the burden of proof. The witness was available. They questioned the witness repeatedly. They chose, they chose, they chose to introduce the evidence through the bar table and not to bring the witness in. They could have brought him in and they could have asked him two or three questions, and we would have had our opportunity to cross-examine him. But to bring in this hearsay evidence and say, There is linkage, when there is not even one shred of evidence that that document -- those documents, those reports, actually made it into the HVO, there is no independent indicia of reliability in order to make a finding on that. So based on that, you have to just ignore it. Finally, on question 10. It's an interesting question, interesting in the sense that here we are, I don't know, nearly 20 years after joint criminal enterprise came into existence, and we're still trying to figure out is it possible or is it probable. We're still trying to figure out the contours. Where are we with joint criminal enterprise, at least with three, the most contentious one of this mode of liability. Now, I don't want to go into the heretical and just remind you that the Supreme Court of the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia, where Justice Mumba, previously Judge Mumba, who sat on the Appeals Chamber in Tadic, agreed with the majority that JCE3 is not included in customary international law. I just thought I'd throw that out. I know it's heretical, and maybe you don't want to hear it, but I have to say it. And I've been meaning to say it and now I have had the opportunity to say it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You already said it in your brief, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me point out, Mr. President and Your Honours, that there's always been this contention, where are the parameters, how far can you extend it. In Brdjanin, as you may recall - you were the Trial Judge, President of the Trial Chamber at the time - there was that issue where Joanna Korner, QC, took a bold step and said, Well, if you're outside the JCE as a physical perpetrator, you can't be -- someone cannot be involved with -- cannot be charged for those events. The Appeals Chamber reversed on that. That caused a bunch of jurisprudence to come out. But be that as it may - be that as it may - even Cassese, the late Cassese, the late Professor Cassese, who has blessed us with this joint criminal enterprise, or cursed us with it, had come to the conclusion that highly likely -- so when we're talking about foreseeability, it has to be highly likely. We're now in the realm of probability. We're in the realm of probability. Now, I know if you look at the Gotovina judgement, you talk about, you say, you, the Appeals Chamber, says "possible." So there's seems to be -- the jurisprudence seems to go to "possible" and yet there this flavour out there that it can't be so extended and so I think the Trial Chamber here took a valiant effort in saying it is probable as opposed to possible because that's one way of containing this far-reaching -- because anything is possible. It's like one of those commercials where you see somebody dropping something and then 20 steps later, some catastrophe occurs. That's joint criminal enterprise. You know, I'm reminded of being a young lawyer questioning a forensic pathologist. I was told that you have to raise doubt. So I'm asking him, Isn't this possible? Isn't this possible? And he's saying, Yes, yes, yes. Finally, after about the fifth or sixth time, the doctor got upset with me. He was annoyed. He said, You're not asking me the right question. I paused. I didn't know what to do. I was told not to ask a question I didn't know the answer to. And the medical examiner then volunteered, Ask me if it's probable, at which point I sat down. What's the point? Anything is possible, but is it probable. But even if you go with the fact that it's possible, now the question is, what do you do about it? We submit, Your Honours, that you must examine all of the evidence. It's not a matter of saying, Well, they acquitted here so now let's convict. You have to assess the evidence, and we submit that you have to go beyond the evidence that was actually looked at by the Trial Chamber, although Judge Robinson reminds us that were you to do a re-evaluation to see other modes of liability or a re-trial on a re-evaluation, you could only do so based on the evidence that was considered by the Trial Chamber and not go beyond. We are suggesting that unless you go beyond what was evaluated by the Trial Chamber, you cannot see the massive amounts of errors and the huge injustice that was done in this particular case, not just to my client but to all of the clients. And that's why, with all due respect, it would be a courageous decision on your part if you decided not to look at the legacy of the Tribunal and say, Well, you know, what would it look like if, after five years of trial and all this money spent, we decided that we have to acquit? What would they say? They would say, This is a Tribunal that has credibility. When somebody is accused or is convicted of capital punishment in the United States where they like to kill people - okay, we have lots of states that have the death penalty - and we have somebody who is right on death row, his head is shaved, and all of a sudden in comes a DNA result that has been hidden. The state doesn't say, You know what? We're going to be embarrassed; maybe we'll even going to be sued. Let's fry the person. Put him on sparky. No. What do they do? They stop the proceedings. Even if it -- somebody has been incarcerated 30 years and there's a potential lawsuit against the state, that's the right thing to do. And the only right thing to do, Your Honours, in this particular case, with all due respect to the Judges in the previous case, is to take the judgement and throw it in the trash bin. That's the only thing that you can do. Otherwise, you have to look at -- I have four minutes. Okay. Otherwise, you have to do an assessment of the entire case. Now, I'm going to surprise you, Mr. President, but I think I'm through with my presentation. I can talk for another four minutes because I'm a lawyer, but I think I've said everything that needs to be said in this particular case. I apologise if I was a little disjointed because of last-minute alterations of my presentation. But I think you heard from Dr. Prlic, he gave you the specifics; I gave you the tour d'horizon. Take both of them, look at our briefs, look at our appeal brief, look at our response, look at our reply, look at the footnotes, and therein lies a reversal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecution response. You have one hour. And then you continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So we will go one hour, then, because it looks like we're about 15 minutes behind. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless you prefer to stop at 1.00, just the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it would be better, no? I think it would be better for everyone if you stop at 1300. That's 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then you will get the 15 minutes later. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. And good morning again to you, Mr. President, Your Honours. May it please the Court. Oh, it is just the afternoon. Okay. The day is flying. Although the week's proceedings have been organised for individual submissions by each of the appellants, this is, after all, one single case. The vast bulk of the crimes were committed as part of a single undertaking, the joint criminal enterprise, to achieve a single goal or purpose, the establishment of a Croat-dominated territory on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what's called the Croatian Community, later the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. And so, Your Honours, before responding to the various -- the many arguments and grounds raised by Mr. Prlic today as well as the other appellants in the coming week, the Prosecution, I would like to first address the overall pattern of crimes, the ultimate purpose behind it all, and why achieving the ultimate purpose led to the criminal enterprise that binds all of these appellants together into a single case, although I will indeed be responding to various points raised already in today's submissions by Mr. Prlic. This will take about 20 to 25 minutes and then I'll turn the floor over to my colleague Ms. Gustafson who will respond to the Prlic appeal itself and to several of the Appeals Chamber's questions as well. Mr. President, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber found that these appellants, exercising their roles and functions within the political and military structures of Herceg-Bosna, are responsible for a multitude of crimes directed against the Muslim population living there during the period of the joint criminal enterprise, January 1993 to April 1994. These crimes followed a "clear pattern of conduct" intended to "ethnically cleanse" the Muslims, to change the ethnic composition of Herceg-Bosna. That's volume 4, paragraphs 65 and 44. Your Honours, the findings of the Trial Chamber are sound. They're amply supported by the evidence of hundreds of victims and eyewitnesses, a huge body of documentary evidence, and by the evidence of many international representatives who told the Trial Chamber what they saw on the ground in Herceg-Bosna and what they heard in their meetings with those responsible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber's findings on the joint criminal enterprise and how the numerous crimes proven at trial fit within it are set out in paragraphs 45 through 64 of volume 4. The pattern makes clear the goal of changing Herceg-Bosna's borders -- sorry, Herceg-Bosna's ethnic composition through crimes. It started in January of 1993 in Gornji Vakuf. The international community had just proposed the Vance-Owen Peace Plan in an attempt to resolve the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. My friend Mr. Karnavas said earlier it was January 1992. It might have been a misstatement. I know he is aware it was January 1993. The plan attributed different parts of BiH, called provinces, to each of the three ethnic groups - Croats, Serbs and Muslims - but protected the rights -- shall I continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It is an only a momentary absence of Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: To each of the three ethnic groups - Croats, Serbs and Muslims - but protected the rights of all ethnicities, regardless of which province they lived in. Seeing an opening in which to advance their territorial aims, Prlic, Stojic, Praljak, and Petkovic quickly seized on the plan, using it as a pretext to ethnically cleanse Muslims from areas attributed to Croats under the Vance-Owen Plan. On 15 January 1993, Prlic, as President of the Government of Herceg-Bosna, issued an ultimatum to BiH armed forces, demanding that they subordinate themselves to the HVO in areas attributed to the Croats. His ultimatum moved down the chain of command, through Stojic, head of the Defence Department of the government; Milivoje Petkovic, who at the time was chief of the HVO Main Staff. He, in turn, dispatched it down to the HVO's operative zones. At that time Praljak was an Assistant Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. He was a Major-General in the Croatian army at the time. Acting as a conduit between Croatia and Herceg-Bosna, Praljak was actively involved in drafting and implementing the Prlic ultimatum. Your Honours heard a reference to that already in this morning's proceedings. I'm referring to volume 4, paragraphs 553, 556, 482. Your Honours have heard this morning references and claims that, in fact, the involvement in the peace process was something that the Croats engaged in as a way of promoting peace. In fact, Herbert Okun, who was the co-chairman on the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia, he was highly involved in the creation, the proposal of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, he testified at the trial and he testified that the HVO's interpretation of the Vance-Owen Plan, as evidenced by this ultimatum was "illegal and contrary to the agreement." Transcript page 16773. See also his evidence at 16775. Rather than embracing the peace process to advance peace, these appellants, in fact, seized on the peace process to advance their territorial aims. When the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina refused to heed the ultimatum and subordinate themselves to the HVO, the HVO attacked, and in the days that followed, HVO armed forces committed many crimes against Muslim civilians and property, torching Muslim homes and expelling the Muslim population throughout much of Gornji Vakuf municipality. Valentin Coric was the Chief of the HVO Military Police Administration. He engaged military police units in eviction operations in Gornji Vakuf. That's volume 4, paragraph 1.000. The next crimes followed the same pattern. On 3 April 1993, Prlic and his HVO government issued another ultimatum, again citing the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, demanding subordination to the HVO by the 15th of April, 1993. That deadline passed and the HVO attacked Sovici and Doljani, the villages in the Jablanica municipality. On 17 April 1993, Muslims were subsequently arrested, detained and then evicted from the villages. There's been a reference to the -- Prlic, as today, claimed that his government had no involvement in issuing ultimatums or that their intentions were benign. In fact, the Chamber's finding linking their government meeting on the 3rd of April, 1993, to the issuance of this ultimatum that then led to the operations in Sovici and Doljani in April is dealt with by the Chamber in volume 4, paragraphs 138, 140, 142. And so on the 17th of April, in co-ordinated attacks on that same day, the HVO forces attacked Muslims also in villages in Prozor municipality the same day they were attacking in Sovici-Doljani. Berislav Pusic was alongside Petkovic on the ground in Sovici and Doljani in early May of 1993, after the villages had been captured by the HVO. He saw the mosques and the Muslim homes which the HVO destroyed after taking the villages. He saw the very harsh conditions in which the Muslim population there was being held. With Petkovic, he facilitated the removal on the 5th of May of the Muslim population, including some 450 women, children, and elderly, out of Sovici-Doljani into territory then controlled by the ABiH. That's volume 4, paragraph 1103. Pusic's JCE role in regard to prisoners increased as the JCE advanced. There was reference today by Mr. Prlic claiming that the policy was that everyone can stay in their homes. That's not what the evidence shows and that's certainly not what the Trial Chamber found. On the same day that Petkovic and Pusic were in Sovici-Doljani working to evict and to remove the Muslim population from those villages, Prlic and Boban were meeting, also on the 5th of May, with a representative of an international humanitarian organisation in Mostar. They asked this organisation to assist them in arranging a big population exchange: Croats from up in Central Bosnia coming into Mostar in exchange for Muslims in Mostar being removed out into Central Bosnia. This organisation refused to get involved in what it called the "creation of ethnically homogeneous zones," and this was something that Mr. Prlic was directly involved in on the 5th of May, 1993. I refer Your Honours to volume 4, paragraph 54, on that. After the successful campaigns in Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, and Jablanica, the Herceg-Bosna leadership and the HVO began its assault on the Muslims in Mostar on the 9th of May, 1993. The summer and fall of 1993 witnessed waves of violent evictions as thousands of Muslims were expelled from their homes, then detained or forced to cross the Neretva River into East Mostar. Valentin Coric 's own military police units participated in the eviction operations and he turned a blind eye to it; volume 4, paragraph 1.000. As did Jadranko Prlic; volume 4, paragraph 121, 171. Stojic was actively involved in organising and conducting the eviction operations. Volume 4, paragraph 355. Pusic also took part in what the Trial Chamber called this "system encouraging the permanent removal of Muslims from West Mostar to East Mostar." Volume 4, paragraph 1116. Your Honours, the population of East Mostar nearly tripled from 20.000 in May of 1993 to some 55.000 by late August of 1993 as the expulsion campaign continued. That's volume 2, paragraph 1200. New measures and crimes would be needed to deal with a large Muslim population dug in on the east side of what was supposed to be the capital of Herceg-Bosna. In June of 1993, therefore, the JCE expanded, as the Trial Chamber found, to include crimes of terror, unlawful attack, and religious destruction linked to the siege, shelling and sniping directed against East Mostar. Volume 4, paragraph 59. After driving the Muslims into East Mostar, each of these appellants contributed to making life there a living hell for them. This siege lasted some ten months, until April of 1994. On 30 June 1993, in response to an attack of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Petkovic ordered the arrest of Muslim males across much of Herceg-Bosna, regardless of their status as civilian or soldier. Thousands of Muslim prisoners found themselves in what the Trial Chamber referred to as a network of HVO prisons, camps and detention facilities. See volume 4, paragraph 980. Coric was one of the architects of this one unified network of HVO prisons. Volume 4, paragraph 982. The network of HVO prisons and camps was then used to serve the goal of removing the Muslims from Herceg-Bosna. The conditions at the prisons and camps, large and small, were violent and appalling. In camps like the Heliodrom, Ljubuski, prisoners were deployed by the hundreds in what the Trial Chamber called a "nearly systematic" HVO programme of using prisoners for forced labour and as human shields. They were forced to dig trenches, carry sandbags into active confrontation lines, all the while being shot at, wounded and killed. It was no better in the smaller detention facilities. An HVO military police report from Prozor dated 18 August 1993 described the horrific conditions for Muslim women detained in the villages of Podgradje, Lapsunj, Duge and Prozor. The report read: "Every day women and girls are taken out from the collection centres ... which are not secure, and taken to houses where they are raped, abused and humiliated. For example, naked women have to serve them, they are beaten until they agree to have sex, and some have their hair shaven off." That's Exhibit P4177, cited at volume 2, paragraph 235, a report of Coric's own military police in Prozor. But the Muslim prisoners did have a means of gaining release from the HVO network of prisons. As the Trial Chamber found in volume 4, paragraph 64, the HVO used its detention facilities as the basis of a "system of deportation" whereby Muslim prisoners could gain their release contingent on their agreement to leave Herceg-Bosna altogether, often with their families. The HVO's release in exchange for deportation programme was administered by Coric's miliary police and proved highly effective in reducing Herceg-Bosna's Muslim population. According to reports of the attaché of the BiH embassy in Zagreb, on 28 and 29 August 1993 alone, nearly 700 Muslim refugees from Ljubuski arrived in Zagreb. They had been released from HVO detention centres on the condition that they leave BiH territory within 24 hours. Volume 2, paragraph 1875. By imprisoning all the Muslim men across these five municipalities, the HVO could more easily expel those left behind, the more vulnerable ones, and that's what happened next. The Trial Chamber considered the organised HVO expulsions of Muslim populations from Stolac, Capljina and Ljubuski municipalities. This is in volume 2, beginning at page 515. The HVO's own statistics showed that the Muslim population in these municipalities dropped dramatically as a result. The Chamber noted, for example, that in Stolac, which had been a Muslim-majority municipality before the conflict, the Muslim population went from 8.093 to zero. That's volume 4, paragraph 57. The crimes did not abate. On 23 October 1993, we saw the notorious HVO massacre of civilians in the village of Stupni Do, in Vares municipality. That's volume 4, paragraph 61. The HVO's highest ranking military commanders, Praljak and Petkovic, attempted to cover up the crime. Volume 4, paragraph 623, 775. This pattern of crime cannot be justified as having occurred during combat operations or some form of self-defence, as some of these appellants have argued. In Gornji Vakuf and Sovici-Doljani, homes were torched, Muslims removed, after the HVO had taken control. Those expelled from their flats in west Mostar and the municipalities of Stolac, Capljina, and Ljubuski, they were not fleeing combat. There was no combat, no ABiH presence. There was only the HVO. These crimes were committed in service of what the Trial Chamber recalled the ultimate purpose. And when one understands the ultimate purpose, one understands, as the Trial Chamber did, that the ethnic cleansing was not a byproduct of the armed conflict. It was an intended consequence of the plan to change the ethnic composition of Herceg-Bosna. The Trial Chamber's discussion and findings on ultimate purpose are set out in paragraphs 6 to 23 of volume 4. Here, the Trial Chamber found that the ultimate purpose was to set up a Croatian entity that reconstituted, at least in part, the borders of the Banovina of 1939 and facilitated reunification of the Croatian people. This entity was either supposed to be joined to Croatia directly, subsequent to possible dissolution of BiH, or otherwise to be an independent state within BiH with close ties to Croatia. So, Your Honours, just a few words here on what the Banovina was and why it matters. The territory of the Croatian Banovina was established by an agreement in Yugoslavia in 1939. Importantly, its territory encompassed not just Croatia but large parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Here we're going to see two maps. And on the left, Your Honours, the map shows a part of Banovina territory in 1939 that fell within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's shaded the olive colour. The Banovina lasted just two years before being swept away by World War II. The map on the right shows the 30 municipalities in BiH that were declared to comprise Herceg-Bosna in November of 1991. Your honours will note the similarity as between the two. There is no coincidence here. 50 years after it vanished, the Banovina territory in BiH was to be restored as Herceg-Bosna. The leading proponent of restoring the Banovina territory on the territory of BiH was then-Croatian President Franjo Tudjman. The Trial Chamber reasonably found that Tudjman advocated dividing BiH between Croatia and Serbia and that he was "preoccupied" with Croatia's borders and the Banovina. Findings at volume 4, paragraphs 10 and 22. US Ambassador Galbraith, who met frequently with Tudjman during 1993, testified that Tudjman believed "that a substantial part of Bosnian territory should become territory of the Republic of Croatia." As Galbraith said, Tudjman "referred specifically and very often to the 1939 agreement that established the Banovina of Croatia that included parts of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina." His evidence is at transcript page 6428. The Trial Chamber also relied on numerous statements of President Tudjman himself on this in what we call the presidential transcripts. Your Honours will be hearing about this throughout the course of this week's proceedings. They're transcripts of recorded meetings that were held in President Tudjman's offices. Scores of these are in evidence, and they memorialise important conversations among many key players. As he said in a meeting with Bosnian Croat leaders in December 1991: "It's time we take the opportunity to gather the Croatian people inside the widest possible borders," cited at volume 1, paragraph 428. Later on the 17th of September, 1992, Tudjman declared that the preservation of Croatian statehood also implies the Croatian Banovina. That's Exhibit P498. Tudjman's many references to the Banovina and Croatia's borders were considered by the Trial Chamber. We refer Your Honours to volume 4, paragraphs 18 and 22. And so this short-lived Banovina was to serve as the vehicle for facilitating the reunification of the Croatian people in Croatia with those in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's the ultimate purpose, and the Trial Chamber's finding on this is fully supported by the evidence. And so what transformed this ultimate purpose into a joint criminal enterprise involving crime on such a tremendous scale? It was the recognition that achieving the ultimate purpose required changing the ethnic makeup of the territories claimed as Herceg-Bosna. It's in volume 4, paragraph 43 that the Trial Chamber makes this very connection. And it's correct to have done so. Here's another map, Your Honours. It shows most of the Herceg-Bosna territory focused on the crime base municipalities. The municipalities shaded blue were Croat majorities before the war based on the 1991 census. Croats did not have a majority in the areas shaded yellow. As Your Honours will note, very substantial amounts of Herceg-Bosna territory in which Croatian people were supposed to be reunified were, in fact, areas in which ethnic Croats were not a majority. The way to ensure that Herceg-Bosna became what it was created to be, an entity for Croats, was to reduce the non-Croat population and to increase the Croat population. The leadership of Croatia and Herceg-Bosna knew this well, even before the common criminal purpose was implemented. I'm going to conclude, Your Honours, by one reference to the evidence that sums up how these -- the joint criminal enterprise actually then succeeded in achieving this goal of changing ethnic composition in Herceg-Bosna. I'm going to go to my very last slide, skipping ahead for time. I want to refer Your Honours to my earlier statement that reference the Chamber's finding on Stolac, which had been a Muslim majority municipality before the war. The finding was that the Muslim population in Stolac went from 8.093 to 0. In volume 2, paragraph 2034, the Trial Chamber recalled the words of Andjelko Markovic, who was the president of the HVO in Stolac. In a meeting with President Tudjman in Zagreb on the 21st September, 1993, latter stages of the JCE, Markovic informed President Tudjman: "Today, there is not a single Muslim in Stolac. We have populated Stolac with our refugees from Bosnia." That's Exhibit P5237. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber reasonably found, and you'll hear throughout our submissions this week evidence and references to the judgement and the evidence that support this, the ethnic cleansing of the Muslim population, whether it's in Stolac or whether any of the other municipalities, all these crimes and the pattern they share shows that the crimes were about changing the ethnic balance to ensure Croats could fully control and dominate the territory of their Croatian community, their Croatian republic. And the crimes, the joint criminal enterprise, as found by the Trial Chamber, corresponded to that goal. And with that, Your Honours, I will turn the floor over to my colleague, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoons.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, as president of the Herceg-Bosna government, Prlic wielded significant power and authority and he used that power to further the common criminal purpose rather than curb it. As Mr. Stringer already mentioned, it was the government's 15 January, 1993, ultimatum, signed into effect by Prlic, that initiated the implementation of the JCE. The ultimatum was implemented down the military chain of command and led to co-ordinated criminal attacks on Muslims in Gornji Vakuf. It was Prlic who then led the government session in April where a second --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- where a second ultimatum was issued triggering criminal attacks on Muslims in Jablanica and Prozor, attacks that followed the same pattern as in Gornji Vakuf. And Prlic was not just a key player in setting the common criminal purpose in motion. He was a key player in ensuring its continuation and the continued flow of Muslims out of Herceg-Bosna. He endorsed the mass arrest of Muslim men beginning in July 1993. He supported the campaign of firing and shelling against the Muslim population of east Mostar while blocking vital humanitarian aid. He also played an important role in what the Chamber termed in volume 4, paragraph 64, a system of deportation by which HVO authorities detained Muslims en masse in terrible conditions and conditioned their release on their agreement to leave for third countries with their families. Prlic justified the detentions and failed to take adequate steps to have detainees released or to improve their detention conditions. And Prlic met repeated international protests of crimes with lies, with false assurances that he would take steps, which he did not take, or false denials. The Chamber relied on countless pieces of evidence in reaching its conclusions on Prlic's responsibility. Evidence including minutes of government sessions, government documents, HVO military documents, and reports from international organisations. And it heard testimony from dozen of witnesses, many of whom were impartial international humanitarian workers who watched the HVO pattern of criminality unfold, protested to Prlic, and received his lies and deflections in response. And what is Prlic's response the Chamber's detailed findings and the voluminous evidence underpinning them? Well, you heard this morning, Your Honours, the crux of his appeal is that the Trial Judgement is a conspiratorial plot, an act of judicial subterfuge designed to convict him under the guise of a reasoned opinion. Then working from this premise of a manipulated judgement, Prlic spends most of his appeal rearguing his case, rarely providing any kind of an explanation as to how no reasonable Trial Chamber could have reached the challenged findings and rarely asserting any kind of legal error. So this conspiracy theory, absurd as it is, is central to Prlic's appeal, because without it he rarely even tries to make a showing of an error warranting appellate intervention. As we've argued in Ground 2 of our response brief, Your Honours, there is no indication that the Trial Chamber disregarded Prlic's witnesses, let alone an indication of a judicial conspiracy. And we pointed out that these claims are propped up on dozens of instances in which Prlic claims the Chamber ignored important evidence from his witnesses but which cite to evidence that was either expressly discussed by the Chamber, is consistent with its findings, or is just irrelevant. And I refer you to our response brief at paragraphs 50 and 53. I would like to address one further argument that was made this morning and also comes up in Prlic's reply brief under Ground 2 at paragraphs 41 to 44, and this the claim that the Chamber provided insufficient reasoning when making adverse credibility findings for three of his witnesses. Prlic does not cite any legal authority for these claims, but there is legal authority on this issue and that authority demonstrates that the Chamber was entitled to make conclusory findings on these witnesses' credibility. I refer you to the Popovic appeals judgement at paragraph 133. Prlic shows no error here. Ground 2 of Prlic's appeal should it be dismissed. I will now move on, Your Honours, to discuss aspects of Prlic's power and authority and his use of those powers to contribute to the common criminal purpose. And in discussing Prlic's JCE contributions, I will respond to questions 3 and 4 raised in your appeal preparation order. Turning to Prlic's powers. The Chamber's findings on Prlic's power and authority as president of the Herceg-Bosna government are based, in large measure, on his formal statutory powers and evidence demonstrating him actually exercising those powers. Prlic argues, and you've heard it this morning, as he did at trial, that despite being president of the government he was virtually powerless. And the general theme underlying this claim, and it's the same theme he tried to convince the Trial Chamber of and failed, is that because he presided over a collective decision-making body, he can't be held responsible for its decisions. Your Honour, the Chamber expressly considered this claim at volume 4, paragraph 89, and reasonably rejected it. It found instead that while the government reached decisions in a collective manner, as the president of this body Prlic played a leading role in the government and held and exercised authority through this collective decision-making process. That's volume 4, paragraphs 90 and 121. And, Your Honours, Prlic effectively concedes the leading role he had as president of the government, and that's clear from paragraph 325 of his appeal brief, where he asserts that his witness, Zoran Perkovic, accurately described how the government functioned. And he cites Perkovic explaining that at government meetings Prlic introduced each agenda item, Prlic opened the discussion, Prlic concluded the discussion by tabling a proposal, and then Prlic ordered a vote, or if Prlic considered the consensus to be clear, he would "simply say, All right, debate over. Regulation adopted." I want to emphasise that this is evidence that Prlic himself relies on regarding his role in the government, and it's the same evidence the Chamber relied on at paragraph 536 in volume 1 in reaching conclusions that track this testimony. The difference is that while Prlic argues that despite this obviously leading role in the government Prlic has no responsibility for its decisions, the Chamber reasonably and logically concluded otherwise. Today I will focus on just one area of Prlic's power and authority, and this is his key role in relations with Tudjman and other Croatian leaders. That conclusion is at the volume 4, paragraphs 119 to 121, challenged in Ground 15 of Prlic's appeal. And I will focus in part on this area, Your Honours, because Prlic's interactions with the Croatian leadership also illustrate his shared intent for the common purpose and the ultimate purpose, and they show JCE members working together to formulate the common purpose and set it in motion. The finding that Prlic played a key role in relations with Croatian leaders is based largely on transcribed meetings that Tudjman held with Prlic and other Croatian and Herceg-Bosna leaders, meetings that show that Prlic as part of the inner circle of Herceg-Bosna and Croatian leaders who discussed and decided their joint goal of creating a Croat-dominated entity in BiH. In challenging this conclusion under Ground 15, Prlic complains that the Chamber only relied on five presidential transcripts. According to Prlic, this is an insufficient number of meetings for Prlic to have a key role in relations with Croatian authorities. That's paragraph 439 of his brief. But Prlic does not show the Chamber acted unreasonably in concluding otherwise. And, of course, the number of contacts is not determinative. The Chamber also rightly also examined the nature of these contacts. I will take you through some of those transcripts that the Chamber relied on. The nature of the discussions in these transcripts illustrate Prlic's key role in relations with the Croatian leadership. As I go through them, Your Honours, I will digress in a few places to respond to some issues raised by the Defence and that relate to the discussions in the transcripts. In finding Prlic's key role in relations with Croatian officials, the Chamber relied, for instance, on P498. This is the transcript of a 17 September, 1992, meeting. Prlic and Mate Boban were among a select group of Bosnian Croat officials to attend this meeting with Tudjman, Susak, and other senior Croatian leaders to discuss "the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatian views on solutions to the crisis." That's page 1. At this meeting Tudjman laid out his geopolitical vision for Bosnia. He made clear that securing the Banovina was necessary to preserve Croatian statehood; that Croatia must secure its territorial position in Bosnia and Herzegovina. To that end, the Herceg-Bosna government they had established must be maintained and that the Croatian entity that they sought to create within BiH must not contain too many Muslims or Serbs. Here are the extracts, Your Honours, where Tudjman makes these key points to Prlic and others. He emphasised that the Bosnian-Herzegovinian question is one of the central issues relating to the Croatian people in general, and "this is not just an issue of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina; it is an issue of the Croatian state, the Croatian people in general. Why? Because this is so relevant to Croatia in terms of history and geopolitics as a result of the unnatural borders of the present Croatian state." That's page 65. And then Tudjman stressed the importance of the language in the preamble to the Croatian constitution "that the preservation of Croatian statehood implies also the Croatian Banovina." Page 67. And he instructed those present that "we have defended Herzegovina with the HVO so that we can establish a Croatian government there and we must keep it." Page 69. Tudjman underscored that it was "in the vital interest of the Croatian people, the Croatian state, that we secure our position in the national and territorial sense in Bosnia and Herzegovina." This morning, Your Honours, you heard Mr. Prlic argue that Herceg-Bosna was a temporary structure, and he argued that the Chamber completely neglected this. The Chamber did not neglect this argument; it expressly considered it at volume 4, paragraphs 7 and 15, and it reasonably rejected it in light of clear evidence, clear evidence like this very transcript where Tudjman emphasised they must keep Herceg-Bosna because it is vital to the national and territorial interests of Croatia. And then Tudjman warned those present that they could not include all Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina in this territorial entity. Why? Because an entity that included all areas in BiH where Croats lived would also include huge numbers of Muslims and Serbs. He said: "We must be alert. If they gave us a border on the Drina with 2 million Muslims and 1.5 million Serbs, whose state would that be?" So he emphasised they should only secure areas of Bosnia that were of "essential interest" to Croatia. That's page 75. He then gave the Herceg-Bosna leadership clear instructions: "In our talks, in your talks, you who are now going to Geneva, therefore, the talks take the position Bosnia and Herzegovina as a community of three constituent nations with the provisions we mentioned earlier regarding the security and territorial sovereignty of Croatia." Your Honours, I see we're at the break time. I can conclude with this transcript or I can break now, as you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
