utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So everyone is here. Let me just check to make sure that we are not missing anyone. Okay, let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, I'd just taken you through some extracts of the 17 September, 1992, presidential transcript. And to sum up on that transcript that the importance of this meeting, a meeting that took place just a few months before Prlic and other JCE members began implementing the common criminal purpose, is apparent. Tudjman gathered Prlic and others among the Herceg-Bosna leadership together and made clear that they must secure and maintain a Croat-dominated entity in BiH. And here I'd like to digress for a moment to respond to an argument raised this morning both by Mr. Prlic and Mr. Karnavas, that Tudjman consistently supported independence for BiH. This argument is in large measure a distraction, because support for an independent BiH is built into the Chamber's findings, and it does not gainsay either Prlic's or Tudjman's support for the ultimate purpose or the common criminal purpose. At volume 4, paragraphs 12, 16, and 17, the Chamber found that Tudjman spoke equivocally, publicly advocating support for an integral BiH knowing the international community was opposed to partition, while nevertheless seeking to create a Croatian entity that would either exist within BiH with close ties to Croatia, or be directly annexed into Croatia. And this public, private divide is perfectly illustrated by the 17 September transcript, because Tudjman emphasises to Prlic and others that it is in the vital interest of the Croatian people, the Croatian state, that we secure our position in the national and territorial sense in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that's at page 74. And then instructs those attending the upcoming talks in Geneva to "take the position Bosnia and Herzegovina as a community of three constituent nations with the provisions we mentioned earlier regarding the security and territorial sovereignty of Croatia." That's page 76. In other words, Your Honours, they must publicly negotiate for a confederal Bosnia comprised of three constituent units, but Tudjman makes crystal clear at this private meeting that the Croat constituent unit Herceg-Bosna is intended to secure the national and territorial interests of Croatia to rectify what Tudjman referred to as the problem of Croatia's unnatural borders. This meeting shows how Tudjman and Prlic's public support for an independent Bosnia with a confederal structure was a step towards achieving their ultimate purpose. And a few weeks after this September 1992 meeting, we see Prlic and other JCE members working to implement the private policy that Tudjman had outlined, namely, securing and maintaining Croatia's territorial and nationality interests by securing the Banovina. In October 1992, Prlic, together with Praljak, who was then Croatia's assistant defence minister, and Stojic met twice in secret with General Ratko Mladic. Petkovic also attended the second meeting. And in accordance with the objectives that Tudjman had articulated, they discussed dividing Bosnia in a way that would further their goal of securing a Croat-dominated entity within the Banovina borders making clear that the Muslims should also get a canton "so they have somewhere to move to." That's P11376 and P11380, both relied on in volume 4, paragraph 119. This material, Your Honour, shows that Prlic is plainly part of Tudjman's inner circle. He attends a key strategy session with Tudjman and works to implement their shared goals through secret negotiations with Mladic, and Prlic maintained this key role throughout the implementation of the common purpose. For instance, Prlic, along Praljak, Petkovic, and Boban attended the 5 November, 1993, meeting, that's P6454, relied on at volume 4, paragraph 119, and discussed at volume 4, paragraph 191. And at this meeting, Tudjman again emphasised the importance of securing a Croat entity in BiH in order to protect the long-term interests of a state of Croatia. He said: "In the military sense, we should see how to protect the interests of the Croatian people and the Croatian state." And he reminded them that they were resolving "the destiny of the Croatian state" for the centuries to come. That's page 20. After hearing Tudjman speak, Prlic explained the importance of the meeting and the importance of himself. He said: "I think that this meeting is extremely important. The highest-ranking officials of the Republic of Croatia and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna are here, and this is an opportunity for open dialogue on the overall situation that we are in and the possibilities to correct the situation that we are in now." That's page 30. And this was not just talk because Prlic then spoke openly about his government strategy of moving ethnic Croats from Central Bosnia into HVO-controlled territory to further their goal of achieving a demographic transformation of Herceg-Bosna. And again I'd like to digress to respond to an issue that was raised this morning, where Mr. Prlic argued that he facilitated this movement of Croats from Central Bosnia into Herceg-Bosna for purely humanitarian reasons. Now, I would add that this is another repeat of a failed trial argument. I refer you to volume 4, paragraphs 197 and 206. Prlic's claims are belied by his own transcribed words at this meeting. He said: "We must move closer to rounding off territories. As a government, last spring, we defined both the proposals and the conclusions, even with regard to moving certain brigades from some areas, which would include moving the population from those areas and concentrating it in certain directions that we think could become and remain Croatian areas." That's page 36. And he added: "I consider that we should now get clear support in social welfare in receiving and accommodating the refugees from Vares. We can objectively in that free area, we can out of our good wishes and political stands, say that all Croats should be down there." That's page 38. So Prlic's own words make clear that even if there was humanitarian aspect to this movement, it was part of a strategy to round off territories by concentrating Croats in areas they thought could become and remain Croatian. The Chamber correctly concluded in volume 4, paragraph 55, that this movement of ethnic Croats was aimed at altering the balance of power so that it favoured the Croats. The Chamber also reasonably relied on this meeting in support of its finding that Prlic played a key role in relations with Croatian leaders. Again, it shows Prlic strategising with Tudjman and other leaders regarding their ultimate shared goal, creating a Croat-dominated territory in Herceg-Bosna. A few months later, at a 13 February, 1994, meeting, P7856, Tudjman gathered what he referred to as the leading people of Herceg-Bosna, that's at page 1, to discuss political strategy. When Prlic spoke part way through this meeting, he said: "Mr. President, the information which was presented today is exceptionally important and of strategic importance, and in some of their aspects fundamentally change certain positions." That's 46. And Prlic declared: "We have created a state of Herceg-Bosna with all systems. Absolutely no solution is acceptable without a Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna, i.e., a Croatian republic, and the borders should encompass as many areas as possible in the whole of Central Bosnia. I believe we can achieve this, by military mean if necessary." That's page 47. Your Honours, this morning Mr. Prlic argued that Herceg-Bosna had no state pretensions and no borders, and Mr. Karnavas argued that it was through subterfuge that the Chamber found that Croatian and Herceg-Bosna leaders were intending to create a state within a state. But it's right here in black and white: Prlic, in fact, insisted on securing an autonomous Croat entity with borders and customs and all systems. Prlic's own transcribed words also contradict his claim in this appeal, that he was not a key player in relations with Tudjman and the Croatian leadership. Prlic expressly recognised the significance of those interactions at the time. He shows no error in the Chamber reaching the same conclusion. Ground 15 should be dismissed. Before I move on to discuss Prlic's JCE contributions, I would like to briefly address an argument Prlic make under Ground 19 that relates to Prlic's interactions with Tudjman and other Croatian officials. And Ground 19 Prlic challenges the Chamber's finding in volume 3, paragraph 567, that Croatian authorities wielded overall control over HVO authorities. And this relates to the international nature of the conflict. As can you see from this transcripts, the transcripts themselves illustrate this control. They show Prlic and other Herceg-Bosna officials reporting to Tudjman, and Tudjman dictating the policy for Herceg-Bosna. I'll just touch on a few further points confirming the Croatian leadership's control over the Herceg-Bosna leadership. First of all, Your Honours, this control was no secret at the time. As Peter Galbraith testified, every diplomat "except the most oblivious clearly understood that Tudjman and Susak controlled the Bosnian Croat political entity, the HDZ in Bosnia, and the HVO," at transcript page 6470 to 6471.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And while Prlic now challenges this control, this contradicts his own repeatedly affirmations of it. Prlic affirmed it, for example, on the 10th of November, 1993, when he and Mate Boban went to Zagreb to seek Tudjman's approval for their proposals to appointments of Herceg-Bosna government ministers. That's P6581, pages 26 to 29, volume 4, paragraph 93. Prlic affirmed Tudjman's control in 1998 when he told Tudjman: "I have been implementing what you were telling me, all the time." To which Tudjman responded: "Well, it is for sure that you were the most intelligent one within that structure." That's P8848, page 8. Prlic even confirmed Tudjman's control directly to the Prosecution in his suspect interview. He told the Prosecution that if Tudjman had wanted to remove Mate Boban, Herceg-Bosna's president and the supreme commander of its armed force, he could have done so in one minute because "the centre of political decision-making was in Zagreb." P9078, page 125. And Tudjman eventually did remove Boban in early 1994. That's volume 3, paragraph 564. But let me be clear, this was not because Boban had been implementing a vast criminal campaign against Herceg-Bosna's Muslims. It was because the international community, particularly the US government, pressured Tudjman to remove Boban. That's volume 3, paragraph 564, citing Galbraith at transcript page 6525 to 6527. And Tudjman himself confirmed this in March 1994 when he told Prlic and others that he had removed Boban from the political scene "but not because I would believe that Boban was guilty." That's P8012, page 57. Prlic's presence is noted at page 3. And Tudjman was not just under pressure to remove Boban at this time. He was also facing immense pressure and threats of sanctions, particularly from the US and UN Security Council, for the continued involvement of the Croatian army in Bosnia. I refer you, for example, to P7789 and Galbraith at transcript page 6520. Faced with what Galbraith termed an ultimatum from the international community in late February 1994, Tudjman was forced to change course and end the war as well as his plans for a Greater Croatia. That's volume 4, paragraph 23, citing Galbraith at transcript page 6519 to 6523, and I refer you also to page 6529. Once Tudjman finally decided to change course, fighting between the ABiH and the HVO immediately ceased. And on the 1st of March, 1994, the Washington Agreement was signed. Volume 1, paragraphs 487 to 488; and volume 3, paragraph 566. In short, Your Honours, the Croatian leadership's overall control over the Herceg-Bosna's leadership is plainly supported by Prlic's own repeated affirmations of it and Tudjman's ability to remove Herceg-Bosna's president and the supreme commander of its armed forces and bring the entire conflict to an end when it suited his political interests. Ground 19 should be dismissed. I will turn now to address Prlic's JCE contributions, and I will focus today on two specific areas of contribution: His contribution to the implementation of the common purpose in Gornji Vakuf, and his contributions to detention facility crimes. If time permits, I will also discuss his deliberate failure to prevent and punish crimes. For the remainder of his JCE contributions, we rely on our brief. I'll begin by addressing Prlic's contributions to crimes in Gornji Vakuf, and in the course of this I will respond to questions 3 and 4 concerning the attack on Dusa village in Gornji Vakuf. As the Chamber found, the implementation of the JCE commenced with the HVO's criminal attacks on Gornji Vakuf. And the evidence the Chamber relied on shows Prlic playing a key role at all stages, beginning with his issuing 15 January, 1993, ultimatum that led to the criminal attacks. And again, I'll digress for a moment to respond to an argument on Prlic's powers. It was an argument raised this morning by Mr. Prlic regarding his limited or to non-existent powers in military matters. But Prlic doesn't challenge the finding that the 15 January government decision, signed by Prlic, was implemented down the military chain of command. And that decision, P1146, which demands that the ABiH in provinces 3, 8, and 10 subordinate to the HVO within five days, states: "This decision shall be implemented by the head of the Defence Department." That same day, Stojic, head of the Defence Department, duly implemented the ultimatum with an order to the Chief of the Main Staff Petkovic and the Chief of the Military Police Administration Coric. That's P1140. Petkovic, in turn, implemented Stojic's order with an order down his chain of command. P1156. The Chamber reasonably relied on these orders, not just to show Prlic's involvement in Gornji Vakuf but also in concluding that Prlic had powers in military matters, including the power to take decisions which had a direct impact on the course of HVO military operations. Volume 4, paragraphs 106 and 111. These documents plainly support this conclusion and they fatally undermine Prlic's arguments in Grounds 11.3 and 12 where he challenges these findings, because these documents show Prlic as head of the government directing the entire HVO military apparatus. Prlic's answer to this order is to pretend it doesn't exist. At paragraph 342 of his brief, he claims neither the HVO HZ HB - that's the government - nor Prlic could issue orders to the head of the Defence Department, but the government ultimatum he signed states, "This decision shall be implemented by the head of the Defence Department." Other examples of orders to the Defence Department are noted at paragraph 212 of our response brief. I'll turn back now to the implementation of this ultimatum in Gornji Vakuf. Here, Prlic does challenge the Chamber's finding that the Gornji Vakuf attack was implementing the government ultimatum - you heard those arguments again this morning - and he does so by simply ignoring much of the evidence the Chamber relied on clearly demonstrating that connection.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Prlic ignores, for instance, P1163, cited at volume 4, paragraph 125. This is a 16 January ECMM report recording Colonel Andric of the HVO Main Staff transmitting Petkovic's order implementing the government ultimatum and demanding the subordination of the ABiH in Gornji Vakuf. He ignores P1185, cited at volume 4, paragraph 125. This is north-west OZ Commander Siljeg's 18 January report sent to the government stating that on 16 January Siljeg and Andric had informed the ABiH in Gornji Vakuf that they must implement the government ultimatum by the 17th, the ABiH had not done so, and the HVO had then attacked Gornji Vakuf. And Prlic ignores the contents of P1227. These are minutes of the government meeting on the 19th, the day after Andric attacked the Gornji Vakuf area. Here, Stojic gave a report analysing the implementation of the 15 January decision in which he noted that "the situation in Gornji Vakuf is calming down." As the Chamber rightly noted in paragraph 127 of volume 4, "that document clearly shows that the HVO itself saw a connection between the ultimatum of 15 January 1993 and the fighting in Gornji Vakuf." Prlic does not engage with this finding. Instead, he just incorrectly claims that these minutes show "the absence of information about developments in the field." That's paragraph 463 of his brief. Prlic has not met his burden on appeal. He ignores key pieces of evidence the Chamber relied on and mischaracterises others. Ground 16.1 should be dismissed. I'll now address question 3 which concerns the killing of seven civilians in Dusa village, Gornji Vakuf, on 18 January 1993. It is uncontested that during the HVO attack on Dusa an HVO shell penetrated the wall of Enver Sljivo's house, a house were dozens of civilians were taking shelter, and that the shelling of the house killed seven civilians; three children aged 3, 11 and 12, three women, and one elderly man. Your Honours have asked to us address the basis for the Chamber's finding that the HVO forces fired on Sljivo's house intending to cause serious bodily harm to the victims which they could reasonably have foreseen could cause their death. As we've indicated in our Stojic and Praljak response briefs, while the Chamber characterised this as an indiscriminate attack, the evidence the Chamber relied on shows that it would be more appropriate to characterise this as a deliberate attack on civilians, because the evidence shows that an HVO tank crew fired a tank shell directly at Enver Sljivo's house which was full of civilians and only civilians, and continued firing as survivors tried to flee. This was a deliberate attack on civilians and the perpetrators had the mens rea for murder. So the Chamber's conclusions on mens rea are correct. The deliberate nature of this attack is made clear from the evidence of the three primary witnesses the Chamber relied on and found credible for this attack, Witnesses BY, BW, and Kemal Sljivo. That's volume 2, paragraph 344. I'm going to go through some of the underlying evidence. Some of this underlying evidence is confidential. I intend to discuss it in open session in a manner that does not tend to reveal the identity of any protected witness. On the morning of 18 January 1993, the HVO attacked Dusa village. They began the attack by shelling the village. That's volume 2, paragraph 358. There was a small group of about 20 local village defenders attempting to defend Dusa. They were located in the woods near the village and had roughly 15 rifles between them. That's Kemal Sljivo, at P10108, page 3; and BW, at 8770 to 8771. I will now show you a photo that should not be shown to the public. This photo, which is Exhibit IC00059, depicts the location of Enver Sljivo's house with a number 1. The house is no longer there; that's the bare patch on the ground. This is the house where the civilians took shelter. And the location of the village defenders in the trees is marked with a 2. And the transcript reference is 8773. The HVO began shelling the village in the morning with mortar and artillery fire. The shelling was aimed both at the defenders and at the village. That's transcript page 8774. After a few hours, at about 12.00 midday, an HVO tank fired on Enver Sljivo's house, killing seven civilians who were taking shelter there. Two witnesses confirmed that a tank fired at the house: Kamel Sljivo, P10108, page 3; and BW, at transcript page 8776. This is further confirmed by Andrew Williams, another witness the Chamber relied on for this attack. He inspected the hole in the house after the attack and assessed that this damage was caused either by a tank or an anti-tank gun. Transcript page 8541. And why is this important? Because it means that the HVO fired directly at the house. Williams explained that a tank is a direct-fire weapon, meaning that the tank crew fires the shells directly at the target with the aid of a site. Transcript page 8541. Philip Watkins, a former artillery officer, gave a similar explanation, as he said "a tank is a precise shelling that is fired and in a direct mode." He added that the target of tank fire "is observed by those firing the weapon." And he explained that tanks shells are designed to penetrate the targeted object. He contrasted tank fire with indirect-fire systems, such as artillery and mortars. Artillery and mortars are not fired directly at the target but are rather fired indirectly by lobbing shells into a general area and are therefore less precise weapon systems. That's transcript page 18861. So the use of a tank for this attack indicates that the house was the HVO's target and they fired on it with a shell designed to penetrate the house. And indeed, Your Honours, there was a line of sight from the tank to Enver Sljivo's house. The next photo, which again should not be shown to the public, indicates this. This is Exhibit IC00058. It shows the location of Enver Sljivo's house in the immediate foreground, it's the bare patch of grass that we saw on the -- bare patch on the ground we saw earlier, and the location of the tank in the background is marked with a red X. That's transcript page 8778. So this confirms the line of sight from the tank to the house. When the tank fired on the house, it was full of civilians and only civilians. There were no soldiers, weapons or village defenders in the house and no shots were fired from the house. That's BW, transcript page 8775 to 8780; and BY, at page 9073. So the perpetrators would have seen no sign of any military activity coming from the house that morning. They would also have known that people were inside because there was smoke rising from the chimney and it was the only house in the village with smoke rising from the chimney. Transcript page 8779 to 8780. And while the Chamber only referred to the single shell that penetrated the house in its findings, evidence from two eyewitnesses the Chamber relied on makes clear that the tank fired at least two shells at the house. BY, at page 9075; and Kemal Sljivo, P10108, page 3. And the shell or shells that were fired after the first hit were fired as women and children were attempting to flee, killing some of the victims as they tried to run away. That's transcript page 9073 to 9075. So the evidence of the witnesses to the Dusa killings that the Chamber relied on to reach its findings demonstrates that the HVO tank crew saw the house, knew there were people in it, fired directly at it with a precise direct-fire weapon, and continued firing as civilians fled. These civilians were deliberately targeted by the HVO. I would add that this attack does not stand alone. It fits squarely within the broader context of an HVO attack directed against civilians across four Gornji Vakuf villages that same day. The Chamber found that the HVO attacks on Dusa, Hrasnica, Uzricje and Zdrimci were carried out in exactly the same manner. The HVO first shelled the villages, destroying some houses. Once inside the village, the HVO arrested the whole population, separated the men, detained all the Muslims, and destroyed their homes. The HVO then removed the majority of the detained civilians. The Chamber reasonably concluded from the absolute similarity of these criminal attacks that they were part of a preconceived plan. That's volume 4, paragraph 704, and also paragraphs 45 and 48. And that absolute similarity is underscored when you compare events in Dusa with events in Hrasnica that same day. When Hrasnica came under attack, a group of 50 civilians similarly gathered in a single house. The HVO proceeded to fire on them from approximately 300 metres away, even though they "could easily see the civilians gathering and taking shelter in the basement of that house." Once the HVO had rounded up the civilians from Hrasnica, they sent a message to the village defenders that "the civilian population would be killed if we did not surrender and give up our arms." That's Senad Zahirovic, P10106, pages 3 to 4; and volume 2, paragraph 372. So the victims in Enver Sljivo's house in Dusa were not an anomaly. They were among a much larger group of victims of a coordinated, violent ethnic-cleansing attack directed against the civilian population of four villages. The Defence teams propose two alternative theories for this attack, neither of which is reasonable on the evidence. The first theory is that the HVO was targeting Muslim defence lines in the village and accidentally hit the house. This claim of an IHL-compliant operation in Dusa involving accidental collateral damage is belied by the fact that the broader HVO attack was directed against the civilian population across four villages. When assessed overall, the Gornji Vakuf attack was conducted with no regard for the principle of distinction, and when you look at it in that broader context and the Chamber's conclusion that the Dusa killing victims were the victims of an indiscriminate attack is correct, because overall this was with an indiscriminate attack directed against village defenders and civilians alike. But in any event, this collateral damage theory cannot be squared with the position of the defenders that day. They were not in the line of fire of the house, and the shells were fired from a precise, direct fire weapon. If we go back to the previous photo, again not to be shown to the public, this shows the location of the tank. So if you're standing facing at the location of Enver Sljivo's house facing the tank, the defenders, Your Honours, would be somewhere off to the left. And that's clear if we then go to the previous photo showing the same location from a different angle, and you can see that the village defenders are not in the line of fire of the house -- or sorry, the other way around, the house is not in line of fire of the defenders. Moreover, the defenders were spread out in a line some 50 to 60 metres apart from one another. Their distance from the house varied from roughly 30 metres away to 100 or 200 metres away. That's transcript page 9077, 9127 to 9129. And they were hiding behind trees. P10108, page 3. So there was no group of defenders that might be visible and logical target for a tank shell. And this Defence theory is impossible to square with the fact that the HVO fired at least two consecutive shells at the house, including on fleeing civilians. If the strike on the house was accidental, they would not have continued firing. The second Defence theory, inconsistent with the first theory, is that the attack on Enver Sljivo's house was justified because Enver Sljivo commanded the village defenders. But of course, that fact alone does not make his house a lawful target. And the Defence does not even allege that Enver Sljivo was in his house at the time or that the HVO had any information indicating that he was. In fact, the information the HVO had at the time indicates the contrary. A 16 January HVO intelligence report states that the Dusa defenders are located in a dugout in the village. 3D00527. And the attack on Dusa had been ongoing for several hours before the tank fired at the house, and during that time as I said no shots were fired from the house. In contrast, the village defenders had been firing back at the HVO. That's P10108, page 3. So this Defence theory, taken at its highest, implies that the HVO was firing highly destructive tank shells at what was obviously an inhabited civilian house with no observable military activity because of a speculative possibility that the owner of the house who commanded the local defenders might be there, contrary to HVO intelligence, and then kept firing as civilians fled. Here I would refer Your Honours to the Appeals Chamber's holding in Galic that: "Attacking anything that moves in a residential building, before determining whether the mover is a civilian or a combatant, is a paradigmatic example of not differentiating between targets." That's footnote 706 of the Galic Appeals Judgement, and footnote 689 of the Strugar Appeals Judgement. That reasoning applies equally to this scenario and shows that this Defence theory, even taken at face value, discloses an indiscriminate attack with a highly destructive weapon. At best, it would be a grossly disproportionate attack given the near certainty of civilian death or injury versus the speculative chance of a military advantage. Either way, this would satisfy mens rea for murder on the part of the perpetrators. But in any event, the evidence does not support the contention that the HVO was trying to target Enver Sljivo with this tank. The absence of any military activity coming from the house and the continued fire on fleeing civilians contradict this theory. So does the broader attack against the four villages, a plainly unlawful ethnic cleansing operation. For these reasons, Your Honours should uphold the Chamber's conclusion that these seven civilians were murdered by HVO forces in Dusa. Unless you have any questions on question 3, I'll move on to question 4. In questions 4 (a) and (b), you've asked that if the Appeals Chamber were to overturn the finding that the Dusa killings constituted the crime of murder and wilful killing, what is the implication for the scope of the common criminal purpose and the mens rea for murder on the part of the appellants under the first category of JCE. In that scenario, Your Honours, the scope of the common criminal purpose and the JCE1 mens rea of the appellants for murder would not be affected. The Chamber included murders during military attacks within the scope of the common purpose because it found that these attack murders were part of the entire system for deporting the Muslim population. Volume 4, paragraph 66. And this finding was based in large measure on the Chamber's overall assessment of the pattern of crimes throughout the existence of the JCE, volume 4, paragraphs 65 to 66 and 70. And that pattern of crimes falling within the scope of the common purpose is a pattern of extreme violence. It includes murder. Not just murder during military attacks in Dusa but also murders arising from the nearly systematic use of prisoners for front line labour and as human shields. It includes cruel and inhumane treatment of prisoners through beatings, appalling conditions, and dangerous front line work. And it includes the mistreatment of Muslims during violent eviction operations, volume 4, paragraph 66. Countless victims were subjected to this pattern of violence, which continued for month after month after month. Overturning just one murder incident would have no discernible effect on this overwhelming pattern of violence, and therefore would not impact the Chamber's conclusion on the scope of the common purpose or the JCE members' mens rea. Even if you look just at the pattern of murders during military attacks, it is clear that overturning the Dusa murder would have no discernible effect on this pattern. As a starting point, regards of how the Dusa killing characterised, the overall conduct of the Gornji Vakuf attacks in January shows the HVO employing extreme levels of criminal violence during military attacks. The nature of those attacks indicates that murder during military attacks was an accepted means of achieving the ethnic cleansing objective from the get-go. As I've already mentioned, the same day as the Dusa attack, the HVO also attacked Hrasnica village and deliberately fired on a group of 50 civilians gathered in a house. After rounding them up, the HVO threatened the civilians with death. And after the Hrasnica defenders surrendered, an HVO soldier opened fire on two of them killing one and wounding the other. That's Senad Zahirovic, P10106, page 4; and P9724, page 4. The Chamber made no findings on this murder, presumably because the victim was not listed in the annex to the indictment, but it found that the evidence of the two witnesses was credible. Volume 2, paragraph 344. We see the same pattern of criminal violence repeated in the next round of HVO military attacks in Prozor and Jablanica in April. These attacks followed the same violent pattern as in Gornji Vakuf and included the murder of two elderly men in Toscanica village, volume 2, paragraphs 89 to 91; volume 3, paragraph 656. By June as the shelling and sniping campaign against the population of east Mostar got under way, murder during military attacks became an even more routine part of the common criminal purpose. For nine months the HVO subjected the Muslim population of east Mostar to a "sustained military attack, including intense, continuous weapons fire and shelling, including rounds of sniper fire over a small, densely inhabited release residential area, with the consequence that many east Mostar inhabitants were injured or killed." Volume 4, paragraph 59. And in terms of shared intent, the Chamber made specific findings that every one of the six appellants, based on their knowledge and involvement, intended, accepted, or encouraged the attack murders in east Mostar. I refer you to volume 4, paragraphs 176, 363, 586, 750, 938, and 1122. These findings, which would stand independently of the Dusa killing, reinforce the appellants' shared intent for attack murders. And these findings, along with the prolonged intense fire on civilians in east Mostar, also underscore the use of attack murders as an intended means of furthering the common purpose. While the attack murders in Mostar were ongoing in August 1993, during an attack on Rastani village, the HVO executed four Muslim men. Volume 2, paragraphs 948 to 963; and volume 3, paragraph 720. On the 28th of October, the HVO attacked Stupni Do and murdered 28 villagers by shooting them, slitting their throats, or burning them in their homes. The cover-up of this massacre, involving JCE members Petkovic, Praljak, and Boban underscores that attack murders were an accepted means of achieving the common purpose. And as I signalled earlier alongside this pattern of attack murders, HVO forces were routinely murdering prisoners by using them for front line labour and as human shields. The Chamber analysed this type of murder independently from attack murders and concluded that it formed part of the common purpose and the Appellants shared the intent for this type of murder. Again, these conclusions would stand independently of the Dusa killings. In summary, the Dusa murder fits within a clear pattern of murders during military attacks, which in turn forms part of an overwhelming pattern of crimes of extreme violence, including two separate types of murder, forming part of the common purpose. Overturning this single murder incident does not disturb this pattern of crimes. The Chamber's conclusions on the scope of the common purpose and the JCE members mens rea are therefore not impacted. Turning now to question 4(c), you've asked about the impact on the mens rea each of the Appellants for murder under the third category of JCE if the Appeals Chamber would overturn the finding that the Dusa killings constituted murder. I will address this question only as it relates to Prlic. My colleagues will answer this question for the other five Appellants in the coming days. There are two parts to question 4(c): First, the impact on the Chamber's JCE3 findings for Prlic; and second, the impact on the Prosecution's arguments under Ground 1. I will address these each in turn, but the bottom line is that there would be no impact because Prlic's JCE3 mens rea for detention and eviction related murders is amply supported by his central role in furthering the common purpose and his shared JCE1 intent for a range of violent crimes. Turning first to the Chamber's findings. The Chamber found Prlic responsible for two murder incidents under JCE3. Detention related murders in Jablanica and a murder during an eviction operation in Mostar in July, volume 4, paragraphs 283 and 284. Overturning the conclusion on the Dusa murder would not impact these findings because the Chamber's reasoning does not turn on whether or not the Dusa killing constituted the crime of murder. For the Mostar eviction murder, the Chamber's foreseeability finding is based only on Prlic's knowledge of and involvement in Mostar crimes. These findings are thus unaffected by the Dusa killing. And in relation to the Jablanica murders in April 1993, the Chamber found they were foreseeable to Prlic based on two factors: First, that Prlic drafted the April ultimatum in the same terms as the January ultimatum; and second, that Prlic was informed of the climate of violence against the Muslim population in Gornji Vakuf and did nothing to prevent or punish the crimes. This finding is unaffected by the Dusa incident. Prlic was clearly informed of the climate of violence in Gornji Vakuf, irrespective of the Dusa killing, through three reports from north-west OZ commander Zeljko Siljeg sent to the government. In that P1206 on the 19th of January, Siljeg reports to the government that several facilities in Gornji Vakuf town and villages "are on fire. The hotel is in flames." On the 28th of January, in Exhibit P1351, Siljeg reports to the government on the seven civilians killed by shelling in Dusa, but he also reports that dozens of houses had been torched or destroyed by shelling in Uzricje, Dusa, and Trnovaca villages. And he reports that the ABiH side is asking for an investigation into the Dusa killings as well as the execution of two civilians in another Gornji Vakuf village, Pajic Polje, and the mistreatment of prisoners in Trnovaca. On 30th of January, Siljeg reports to the government that "the houses, stables, and primary school have been burned down or demolished" in Gornji Hrasnica. In Donja Hrasnica, most buildings have been burned down or demolished, and there is no civilian population left in Gornji Hrasnica and Donja Hrasnica. He adds that some of the population were taken prisoner and taken to Trnovaca and some fled to Grnica. That's P1357. This climate of violence surrounding the Gornji Vakuf attacks is apparent from these reports regardless of how the Dusa killing is characterised. Siljeg reports in a matter-of-fact manner on the widespread torching of homes, the detention, murder, and flight of civilians, and the mistreatment of detainees. And Your Honours have specifically asked for submissions on whether Prlic was privy to the contents of Siljeg's 28/29 January report, P1351. As we've indicated in our brief, the Chamber reasonably found that Prlic was informed of the contents of all three of Siljeg's reports, volume 4, paragraph 132. These reports were specifically addressed to Prlic's government. As the Chamber noted, the reports discussed the HVO operations launched pursuant to the 15 January ultimatum that Prlic had signed. The Chamber also noted that Prlic had met with Stojic, who was also an addressee on Siljeg's report, about the implementation of the ultimatum. And more generally, evidence the Chamber relies on shows that Gornji Vakuf was the most pressing matter for Prlic and the government at the time. That's volume 4, paragraphs 125 to 127 and 129. At trial Prlic did not claim that he did not receive or read Siljeg's reports. To the contrary, in his Rule 84 bis statement he said: "The period that followed the 15th of January is the only period in which the HVO HZHB," that's the government, "emerged as one of the addressees when information was submitted on the situation that was unfolding in Gornji Vakuf." So Prlic has conceded that these reports were not just addressed to the government. They were submitted to the government. The contention that Prlic did not bother to acquaint himself with official military reports submitted to his government that concerned the most pressing issue at the time, a contention he never made a trial, is implausible. The Chamber reasonably concluded otherwise. But it's also important to step back from the specific contents of these reports for a moment because, as we've argued in our appeal brief, Prlic's awareness of a risk of JCE3 crimes should not depend on his knowledge of specific crimes in specific locations. His ability to foresee the possible commission of JCE3 crimes, murders in particular, arises in large measure from his central role in planning and implementing a campaign of violence against the Muslim population of Herceg-Bosna. As of October 1992, Prlic was one of the leaders who sought to change the ethnic makeup of Herceg-Bosna, including by moving out its Muslim population. Volume 4, paragraph 43. For the next year and a half from one of the top leadership positions in Herceg-Bosna, Prlic facilitated and supported a vast criminal campaign. A campaign whereby HVO forces systematically attacked Muslims through a range of violent crimes. The extent of violence necessary to achieve this sweeping demographic transformation was apparent from the pattern of crimes that played out and inherent in the goal itself, the goal of forcing thousands of Muslims out of their homes and villages and out of Herceg-Bosna altogether. So to conclude our answer on question 4(c) in relation to Prlic, Prlic's JCE3 mens rea for murders is amply supported by his central role in the common criminal purpose and his shared intent for crimes forming part of that purpose, and it is augmented by the many direct reports of violent crimes he received. And I refer you to our appeal brief at paragraph 57. And with that, Your Honours, I'll turn back to Prlic's JCE contributions and in particular his contributions to detention facility crimes. And this relates to Grounds of Appeal 16.7 to 16.11 and Ground 13. In essence, Prlic knew the detention facility conditions were poor. He sought to deflect international attention, took inadequate measures to improve conditions, and facilitated the systematic expulsions that this network of prisons was designed to achieve. The Chamber made reasonable findings that are firmly grounded in the record. I'll take you chronologically through some of Prlic's conduct relied on by the Chamber, conduct that illustrates Prlic's powers in this area, his knowledge of criminal conditions, and his contributions to this system of detention, mistreatment, and expulsion. On the 8th of June, 1993, Prlic signed the government decisions establishing Gabela prison in Capljina and appointing Bosko Prevesic as its warden. Volume 4, paragraph 251. Gabela was then used over the next six months or so to detain thousands of Muslims in terrible conditions and then funnel them out of Herceg-Bosna. Conditions so inadequate that some detainees resorted to drinking their own urine. Volume 3, paragraph 221. Gabela detainees were routinely abused and some murdered, including by the warden Prlic had appointed, Bosko Prevesic, who regularly beat detainees and murdered a detainee after discovering a piece of bread on him. Volume 3, paragraphs 237 and 251. Prlic was well aware that Muslims being unlawfully detained and subjected to poor conditions of detention. On the 6th of July, 1993, days after the HVO began implementing Petkovic's mass arrest order, Prlic met with representatives of the international community. He acknowledged that 6.000 men had been detained simply because they were of military age. He also admitted that the HVO was unable to look after this many detainees. Volume 4, paragraph 153. And his admission is borne out by a multitude of factual findings demonstrating the severe overcrowding and other deprivations common to HVO prisons. At this 6 July meeting, Prlic told the internationals that the HVO had decided to release the detainees. But, as found by the Chamber, these releases were transformed into a system of forcible expulsion. Detainees could secure their release from detention in terrible conditions if they agreed to depart for third countries. Volume 4, paragraphs 153 and 64. Prlic was not just aware of this expulsion system; he actively worked to further it. On the 16th of July, just ten days after the meeting I have just discussed, Prlic, with two other Herceg-Bosna officials, informed an international organisation that they were going to negotiate with ODPR Croatia to obtain 10.000 transit visas for Muslims they claimed "wished to leave," but which included men then detained. They then asked the organisation to help them implement their plan by establishing transit centres for Muslims wishing to go abroad. The organisation refused to assist in what it correctly assessed was an ethnic-cleansing plan. Volume 4, paragraph 234. A few days later, Prlic chaired two government sessions on 19 and 20 July, where the problems of overcrowding in Capljina prisons, that's Dretelj and Gabela, were discussed. In the minutes the government recognised that the existing conditions violated international law, and while the government discussed identifying new detention facilities, what was actually done was that roughly 700 prisoners were sent from Dretelj to the Heliodrom which the Chamber noted was overcrowded throughout its operation, while the remaining Dretelj and Gabela prisoners continued to languish in appalling conditions. I refer you to volume 4, paragraphs 248, 253 to 255, and 268. This photo, Your Honours, shows effects of the conditions we are talking about here. This is P4588, page 9. These are Dretelj detainees who were transferred to ABiH-held territory in late August after just two months of detention. That's volume 3, paragraph 71; and Witness BQ, at page 7908 to 7914. This shows the deprivations they were subjected to, deprivations that Prlic could have alleviated if he responded appropriately to the reports brought to his attention. Nearly a month after these government sessions in July, on 16 August 1993 a representative of the international community informed Prlic that Heliodrom detainees were being sent to work at the front and some had been wounded while working. Volume 4, paragraph 229. What does Prlic do with this alarming report? Nothing. Volume 4, paragraph 232. By the time of the 5th September government session a few weeks later, images of Dretelj detainees, like the one you just saw, had been broadcast internationally. Volume 3, paragraph 71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Herceg-Bosna and Croatian leaders are facing international pressure regarding detention facilities. For example, volume 4, paragraph 604, and P9507, cited at volume 3, paragraph 562. This international pressure is reflected in the minutes of the 5 September government session where the government concludes that mistreatment and poor conditions in detention facilities have become "harmful to the reputation and interests" of Herceg-Bosna. That's P4841, relied on at volume 4, paragraphs 219 and 244. The government claims at this session that it is not responsible for the present situation but it nevertheless decides to take action "in order to avoid the situation being used in ways that are adverse to the political and other interests" of Herceg-Bosna. Then the government issues tasks to various departments, tasks that on their face are aimed at improving detention facility conditions. However, as the Chamber reasonably found, these actions were inadequate because the bad conditions continued for many months more; indeed, the day the centres were closed down, well into 1994. Volume 4, paragraphs 219 to 220. These government minutes are telling. Prlic has known for months, as the documents demonstrate, that detention facility conditions are inadequate, yet he is spurred to take action - inadequate action - by international scrutiny that could harm the political interests of Herceg-Bosna. In his appeal, Prlic does not even engage with the Chamber's conclusion that this government session reflects Prlic's insufficient and inappropriate response to detention facility crimes. Instead, he tries to affirmatively rely on these minutes as an example of his and the government's effort to combat crimes. He just disregards the Chamber's contrary conclusion. I refer you to paragraph 621 of his appeal. Prlic's disingenuous response to detention facility crimes is reinforced by a letter he wrote on 2 December 1993 to Cedric Thornberry, P7008, relied on at volume 4, paragraph 262. Prlic professes in this letter his readiness to establish the facts about what he calls "the possible incorrect treatment of detainees" which, of course, he knows is not possible but actual, and he knows it's not just incorrect but criminal. He then states as a sign of goodwill that the government has decided to unilaterally release several hundred detainees and this goodwill promise of release was also a ruse. As I've already noted, the supposed release of detainees was, in fact, a system of deportation. And, indeed, shortly after making this promise to Thornberry, Prlic's government is sent a string of reports from Berislav Pusic, who is head of the government's exchange services implementing Boban's 10 December decision to close detention facilities. The statistics in these reports demonstrate that the vast majority of the purportedly released detainees are being sent to ABiH-held territory or to third countries. I refer you to P7178, P7185 P7246 and P7468; and volume 4, paragraph 1131. The sample of the evidence I've just reviewed amply supports the Chamber's conclusion, at volume 4, paragraph 273, that Prlic knew about harsh conditions in HVO detention facilities, and nonetheless justified the detentions, denied the situation was bad, and on occasion took inappropriate measures and allowed the detainees to be moved to ABiH-held territory or third countries. Prlic's challenges to the findings on his contributions to these crimes largely boiled down to a repetition of his failed trial argument that he had no power over these facilities. We've responded to these claims in detail in our brief. Today I'll just underscore one point on this issue: Prlic says now that he had no power but he did not make this claim at the time. At government sessions discussing detention facilities, the government doesn't claim it has no power to act; it claims it's not responsible but then exercises authority and demonstrates its power to intervene, albeit with inadequate measures. And when interacting with internationals who are protesting to Prlic about detention facility crimes, Prlic doesn't say, Don't look at me, I have no power. To the contrary. He promises to act, to release detainees, to close detention facilities, to bring perpetrators to justice. He did not follow through on these promises, but he consistently held himself out as having the power to address detention facility crimes. Grounds 13 and 16.7 through 16.11 should be dismissed. Unless Your Honours have any further questions, that concludes my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That brings me now to Mr. Karnavas. You've got 30 minutes, starting from now, to reply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One moment. Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you going to share again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but we're going to reverse roles. I'm going to go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. You have got 30 minutes. Your client -- I'm not going to stop him, of course, but I think your client should understand that when he engages a lawyer, he should leave it in the hands of his lawyer. But anyway, let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, good afternoon. Just as facts get in the way of a good story, so do inconvenient truths interfere with a purpose-determinative narrative. Now, I'm going to start from where my learned friend ended and then I'll go back to the beginning of the Prosecution's presentation. "People, citizens of Mostar, you have to understand that this is a judgement day when you have to start with fight. I'm inviting citizens who can bear a rifle, who can bear a rock, to kill Ustasha. We shall keep on. We shall not stop until there is a single Ustasha left." Now, for those who may not know what an Ustasha is, that is the pejorative term for Croats during this period. Of course, the term goes back to World War II. I'm not going to give a history lesson. I think we all know that. But when were these words spoken and by whom? This is June 30th, 1993. This is in Mostar. This is in Mostar. And these are the words of Commander Pasalic. Halilovic was the one that actually said, "We shall keep on. We shall not stop until there's a single Ustasha left." On June 30th, this was on Radio Mostar so everybody could hear. All the Croats could hear. The peace-loving ABiH, this is their approach. At the same time while they were supposed to be working with HVO, these are the remarks that are being made. And you must understand - and others will talk about this - that there was an act of treachery where the HVO soldiers were killed by their comrades, Muslims that were serving in the HVO. They were doing the handiwork of the ABiH. And this was what precipitated many of the events that follow after June 30th. Be that as it may, it has to be very clear -- and the evidence is there. We have it all. Look at what we've cited. I'll go back to what I said earlier: The HVO HZHB could not issue orders to the military. Mate Boban was the President of the Presidency, so he was above the government. Only he could order the military. Dr. Prlic never orders anybody. The fact that he presides over these meetings, okay, what does that mean? It is not up to Dr. Prlic to decide what is going to be on the agenda. Everybody proposes. He has no authority not to include something on the agenda. So where is the power? He doesn't appoint. He has no authority to appoint someone. The fact that he signs the appointment, even if he doesn't agree with the appointment, doesn't make it his appointment. No more so when the President of a Bench signs a decision or a judgement where he or she is in the minority. It is not the President's judgement; it's the Trial Chamber's judgement. But to keep this mantra, Prlic orders, Prlic decides, Prlic this, Prlic that, is all nonsense. Now, I'm going to go back to where we started and this thing about ethnic -- to change the ethnic composition. Now, some people read the newspaper and say, Bosnia this, Bosnia that. The country's name is Bosnia and Herzegovina. They are two different regions. And there is no way on earth that you're going to make a Central Bosnian Croat into a Herzegovinian. It's just nonsense. They're different. They're about as close as a southerner from the deep south to a New Yorker. So this nonsense about trying to homogenise Herzegovina when 95 per cent of Herzegovina was resided by Croats. This nonsense about reverse ethnic cleansing, what the Prosecution doesn't say and what the Trial Chamber ignores completely, that the Croats in Central Bosnia were rounded with the Mujahedin on their door-steps. And, yes, they wanted to get them out. The Prosecution's theory and the Trial Chamber's conclusion is that they were reversed -- they reverse ethnically cleansed the Croats from Central Bosnia so they could repopulate Herzegovina. Where do those Croats go when they finally escaped? They went to Croatia. Why? There was no room in Herzegovina by that point. There were so many refugees from everywhere and displaced persons. They went to Croatia. So it wasn't some evil plot to get those people out of there, to plant them in Herzegovina, and somehow a Central Bosnian Croat would go up or his seeds would grow up to be Herzegovinian. Nonsense. Tudjman and Banovina, no doubt he had an obsession. Well, when I look at the map, too, as a Greek, I look at Asia Minor and say, Yeah, Constantinople is ours, the coast is ours. But that's -- historically you can look at it, but it's no more ours today than it will be tomorrow. Tudjman looked at the Banovina, referenced the Banovina, and in 1991, as I indicated, was thinking of what would happen if Bosnia-Herzegovina fell. Now, the Prosecution keeps harping about this one presidential transcript. So right before this presidential transcript, on August 17, 1992, Dr. Prlic gives an interview. It's 1D02078. The interview is in Split. Joining him was a fellow named Jure Pelivan, and he was the President of the Government of BiH at the time. He's a Croat living in Sarajevo. He's from Sarajevo. I don't know if he is still alive these days. But in there, Dr. Prlic explicitly talks about what this temporary -- he says: "The Croatian Defence Council is a civilian authority; namely, the temporary executive government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and that much should be clear." He goes on and he says: "The temporary executive government was elected to be the President of the War Presidency of the municipality assemblies, ensuring in that way the legitimacy of that temporary executive government. In all its documents, it emphasises that all of them are temporary documents. It adopts interim measures. It complies with the legislation of the republic. In the preamble of all its decisions, it refers to decisions concerning the introduction of the state of war, the imminent threat of war, and the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina," echoing what Dr. Prlic said this morning. Now, this is an interview in 1992, in August, the 17th, one month before this famous September conversation that they have in Zagreb, and I'm going to get to that. He goes on to say: "I believe that a Constitution ... one road, one direction towards sustaining the statehood of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the materialisation of the interests of equally the Croatian and the other constituents peoples living in it." Nothing about carving up. Nothing about grabbing. Nothing about joining Croatia. "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna fully respects that proposal of the Constitution. We have to organise everyday life." Remember, I was saying, it's a failed state. Bosnia-Herzegovina has failed. It doesn't exist as a state. For all intents and purposes, nothing is functioning. That's why the municipalities had to take actions on their own. "We have to organise everyday life. Our economic, financial and every other system in Bosnia-Herzegovina has collapsed." And it goes on. You can see it for yourselves, Your Honours. But now let's go to this famous 17th September, 1992. We heard so much about it, and it's interesting. During the trial, the Prosecution had, because of their limited resources, I suspect, had only translated parts of it. It turns out that the parts that they translated gave a one-sided picture. And that's the whole problem with this judgement. Oh, sitting there. And if I didn't know any better, I would have bought everything they just said because it sounds good. But there's another side to the story. In that same meeting where Prlic is sitting there listening to Tudjman, and I would imagine it's a like a meeting where you're sitting around and there's President Trump saying all sorts of stuff, but who knows whether you can take him seriously or not. But can you really be associated with what that person is saying and saying that those are your -- you're adopting those because you're sitting there politely saying nothing? But this is what Prlic says. In this document, which is 1D00397, I believe that's the document. If I'm not -- I'll correct the record. I'm sorry. It's P00498. Sorry about that. And I'm referring to paragraphs 28 to 29. "It has been clear to me ever since I became involved in this and since I have been in this post. This aim is the forming and ordering of Bosnia-Herzegovina in accordance with the principles of the European community." He is saying this in front of Tudjman. "This is the constituting of Bosnia-Herzegovina through three national units. I think that is -- that is convenient for the Croats, but the national composition of the population should not be the only criteria. I would like to say that this is -- that this part we have generally succeeded in defending the Croatian areas except in the Bosnian Posavina." Well, what are we talking about defending the Croatian areas? Croats have been living there for generations. And those are the areas where, just like the Serbs, and just like the Bosniaks, they've been situated there. So they're defending the areas, whether it's Posavina, whether it's Central Bosnia, whether it's Herzegovina. And they're all different even though they're part of the same country. They have -- they're different. Just like a New Yorker is different from somebody from Mississippi. Now we go to further on. He says: "We have organised the authorities. This is only starting. We have an Official Gazette." Why as an Official Gazette necessary? So everybody could know what the laws were. And guess what, news flash: Every municipality had a gazette prior to the war. Second news flash: Ribicic, the constitutional expert from Slovenia, and Slovenia was part of Yugoslavia, and I might have missed that the day of class, but he claimed that by having a gazette, the Croatian community and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna took on state-like qualities when every municipality had a gazette. And that shows you how the gentleman was discredited, but none of that is taken into consideration. Anyway, we go on: "We are passing necessary decrees. We are trying to take care -- and to take care of the citizen aspect in the liberated territories. Why is this important? It is important because it is a disorganised situation. People will join those who are organised if we set up our institutions through the" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sorry. "If we set up our institutions through the SDK, the social accounting service," that's the payment bureau I was talking about earlier. Because the payment bureau, the way it worked, money would go from the municipalities to the state, and then from the state it would go back down in these itemised budget areas for education, and for garbage, for this and that and the other. That stopped because -- and we brought in a witness who testified that if the electrical grill and the telephones are not functioning, that system cannot work, which is why they had to make provisions from -- for themselves. So if you are going to look at that transcript, I invite your close scrutiny and attention to all of it, or at least also the parts that we make reference to. Not just the one-sided part. And I understand they have a limited budget, they can only translate what is convenient for them which is why they limited the translations on many of the things that they did during the trial. Now before I go on and before I forget, there was one point I wanted to react but I know we're in an appeal court, and so I tried to keep my -- to try to stay calm, not to get over-excited. But at one point my learned friend said that "a contention never made at trial," as if we have a burden of proof. We have no burden of proof. If they wanted to bring in Siljeg, they could have. Now they tell him that he did this, he did that, his reports are so great. Why not bring the gentlemen in if this is the genesis - the start, that is - of the JCE, and this guy is the bearer of truth and his reports are to be accepted, and we can get from him why he sent it to the government, why he copied the government, why would they bring him in? They questioned him. He was available. They got his diaries. Instead, well, if you can't go through the front door, maybe through the basement window, through the bar table motion. And now they say: Accept this as the truth without any proof that that was actually delivered during that period of time. Now, I want to speak about January 15th. Let me go back a little bit. We already said that on the 2nd, 3rd of January, fighting began in Gornji Vakuf. Began right after the new years because the Croats during Christmas and new years, they like to fly their flag and they weren't able to do so during the Communist era. They would have to celebrate privately because Tito wasn't a big fan of religion. And all of this came out, this is all testimony, so it's not Karnavas testifying. And then around the 6th, things are picking up. This is sort of craziness of soldiers drinking and getting out of control. By the 11th we said there was actual fighting. I've already told you on the 2nd and on the 10th in Geneva what is happening, and when Izetbegovic -- just as Boban would go to Geneva, some of their generals would go there because there was a political component that Attacari [phoen] hosting -- not hosting but he was directing, and there was a military aspect. And there was Nambiar I believe, General Nambiar was the gentleman's name, and he would sit there and they would talk about military matters. But on the 10th -- okay, 11th is the fighting in Gornji Vakuf. On the 10th, Enver Hadzihasanovic, the commander of the 3rd Zenica Corps, issued an announcement applying pressure on the Muslim leadership to reject the internal organisation of BiH into three constituent units, because by that point, the framework -- the Vance-Owen Peace Process, VOPP as client would like to say, was already out. That this was -- this was in the making, okay? And so he is saying he's against that. And this is 4D0123, and I believe we made reference to this in our brief in I want to say 16.1.3. And here is what the gentleman says: "On the occasion of political negotiations in Geneva and on request of huge number of units and fighters of the 3rd Corps of B and H Army, we offer you our unconditional support in our office to prevent division of B and H on ethnic or any other principle. Do not allow, neither shall we, that the blood spilled so far and the sacrifices of our fighters, children, women, fathers, and mothers be in vain." That's on the 10th. That is on the 10th. So is it any wonder, is it any wonder that on the 11th, there's fighting? So, is it a coincidence or is there a convergence. Now on the 13th of January, so two days later after there's the fighting, there's a document, P0115, where General Petkovic, and I'm sure they're going to talk about it, and I don't want to steal their thunder, and they know much more about this, but at that point he requested that the situation be calm and to analyse the reasons for the conflict. The 11th, it starts: "It's really getting out of control. Remember, the enemy are the Serbs. These are two friendlies. They're working together. They're part of the armed forces of BiH." And General Petkovic is saying we need to figure out what is going on and calm down the situation. Then we have the 15th, as I indicated, the Zagreb Agreement. But here's Boban, here's Boban January 15th, by serendipity, P01158 - we mention this in our brief in 16.1.1 - here is Boban saying, at any cost, one should listen to reason and make comprises and accept certain concessions in order to stop the war and make Bosnia and Herzegovina the state foreseen by Izetbegovic in his speech when he said that tomorrow it should be a free country with a free flow of people and capital. Incompatible with this thinking is the claim that any territorial organisation means giving something to someone when Bosnia and Herzegovina is a unified whole. Nobody can give anything to anyone. Everybody has equal rights, and their rights have been determined by arguments. That's VOPP. That is VOPP in its clearest forms. But this is Boban, on the 15th. This is when the Zagreb Agreement is reached and when General Praljak comes down to Mostar. Now the situation happens in Gornji Vakuf and we submit that if you look at the evidence closely, the situation in Gornji Vakuf is out of control. This 15th agreement was for the purposes of stopping, not of escalating and certainly not of the start of some joint criminal enterprise because, Your Honours, the evidence is overwhelming. During this period throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, you had HVO and ABiH co-operating, joint commands, fighting together in other parts. And we submit that Gornji Vakuf is sort of representative of what's happening in the conflict between these two armies and these two peoples; that in situations things are getting out of control and then they would have these meetings, they would have joint commands, and so on and so forth. It's a little bit like what is happening in Syria, with all these different factions trying to figure out a way to move forward. And there's starts and fits, but there is -- this is not representative of a joint criminal enterprise. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have just under seven minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're breaking my heart, Mr. President. Okay. I'll move quicker. On 18 January, 1D01521, there is a letter that was sent by Boban and Ahmagic [phoen], where they're saying, "We also have evidence showing that on the basis of an order" -- this is to Izetbegovic. "... on the basis of an order of your highest leadership, the Army of BiH prepared, planned, and carried out the attack on HVO units and civilian population in Gornji Vakuf." This is meriting some consideration, so what we're saying is there's evidence that you should look at, not just what the Prosecution points you in that direction. Just a couple of closing remarks, Your Honour, and then perhaps Dr. Prlic will -- can get his points in as well. I'm reminded, thinking about all of this, our biggest challenge was, how do we convey this picture to you all. This was a five-year trial. It's 12 years that I have been working and living with this case. Very complicated. How do we convey the mistakes, the errors, the omissions, the commissions, that were made in this particular case? How do we get you into the picture so you can see the challenges? The Prosecution has done exactly what they have done in their brief: The echo what is in the brief and they say, See, the Trial Chamber found that. Well, of course they found that because they only looked at one piece of the evidence. And we're saying, Don't take the easy way, don't adopt their approach; but, rather, look at all of the evidence. That is the simplistic path of least resistance. Just read the judgement. We say that would be manifest injustice if you were to do that. And I'm reminded of the words of Justice Stewart in the U.S. Supreme Court in Jackson vs. Virginia - it's a short quote - because I think it goes to what we're talking about: "Any evidence is relevant -- that has any tendency to make the existence of an element of a crime slightly more probable than it would be without the evidence -- could be deemed a 'mere modicum.' But it could not seriously be argued that such a 'modicum' of evidence could, by itself, rationally support a conviction beyond a reasonable doubt." Wise words. And what we're saying is, you have to just -- you have to look at the other evidence that was part of the record, not just what the Prosecution is citing because they're citing the Trial Chamber and we're claiming they ignored our evidence and we've given you -- as I said earlier, we've given you all the citations. They claim we didn't give you citations today; we just make arguments. There are over 2.600 footnotes, and I would say there are over 10.000, if not 15.000 references to the record. We're asking you to please not take the easy way that the Prosecution is asking you to do. Look at the evidence, and we're confident - we're confident - that you will reach the right decision, and the only decision in this case is a complete reversal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Prlic, you have three minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to use break to have short consultation with my client [sic] because it was scheduled like that. But if it is three minutes, I just want to make one proposal. Collective way of decision-making is mentioned, that. I stay behind all decision of HVO HZHB, all the decision of government of HRHB. I made least of all those minutes introduced in dossier. And I suggest, if you accept, I'm going tomorrow to bring list of all meetings, 80 of them. This is the only way for me to make any decision. And then make your judgement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That doesn't mean to say that I'm giving you permission to do that, by the way. That brings today's hearing to an end. We will reconvene tomorrow at 9.30, like today. The timetable, the schedule, will be a little bit different. The first break will be longer. Otherwise, we stick to the same schedule which has been communicated to you. So 9.30 tomorrow morning, and it will be Mr. Stojic's Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, 21 March 2017, at 9:30 a.m.
